questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has a routine complete blood count before a dental procedure. She feels well and her pregnancy has been uncomplicated. Her hematocrit is mildly lower than it was before pregnancy, and her physician tells her the finding is expected. Which of the following best explains this laboratory result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An absolute fall in red blood cell mass below baseline

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow suppression caused by rising estrogen levels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased splenic destruction of maternal red blood cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Plasma volume expansion exceeding red blood cell mass expansion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of erythropoietin release by placental hormones

explanation.summary: Physiologic anemia of pregnancy is dilutional: plasma volume rises more than red cell mass.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood volume rises 40%-50% in pregnancy, but red blood cell mass rises only about 20%. Because the plasma expands more than the red cells, hemodilution lowers the hematocrit, producing the physiologic anemia of pregnancy. Hemodilution actually stimulates erythropoietin, so red cell production increases even though the hematocrit stays below nonpregnant values.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Red blood cell mass rises by about 20%; it does not fall below baseline.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No marrow suppression is involved; red cell production actually increases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pregnancy anemia is not hemolytic; the lecture attributes it to hemodilution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythropoietin is stimulated, not suppressed, by the hemodilution of pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 22 weeks' gestation notes that her breasts have enlarged substantially, yet she has had no milk production. Histologic study of breast tissue at this stage would show fully developed alveoli capable of secretion. Which of the following hormones is chiefly responsible for preventing milk production at this point in pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estradiol

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxytocin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progesterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolactin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxin

explanation.summary: High progesterone levels hold milk production in abeyance during pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: The breasts are developed enough to make milk by about 10-12 weeks, and prolactin drives alveolar differentiation into secretory epithelium by about 18 weeks. Milk production is nonetheless blocked throughout pregnancy by high levels of progesterone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Estradiol contributes to early breast enlargement but is not the hormone blocking lactation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxytocin is not described as suppressing milk production during pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolactin promotes alveolar differentiation and polyamine production; it does not block milk production.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin acts on pelvic ligaments and vasculature, not on milk production.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 12 weeks' gestation has thyroid function tests drawn at her first prenatal visit. She has no palpitations, heat intolerance, tremor, or weight loss. Her total thyroxine is elevated, while her free thyroxine is within the normal range. Which of the following best explains these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune thyroid gland hyperfunction with excess hormone release

choices.label: B
choices.text: Estrogen-stimulated hepatic production of thyroxine-binding globulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placental lactogen-driven rise in unbound circulating thyroxine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progesterone-induced suppression of thyroxine-binding globulin synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxin-mediated reduction in hepatic clearance of thyroxine

explanation.summary: Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, increasing total thyroid hormone while free hormone stays stable.
explanation.whyCorrect: In pregnancy, estrogen stimulates the liver to make more thyroxine-binding globulin. More binding protein raises total thyroid hormone levels, but free (unbound, active) hormone remains relatively stable, so the patient is euthyroid.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A normal free thyroxine and absent symptoms argue against true hyperthyroidism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placental lactogen affects insulin resistance and lipolysis; free thyroxine is normal here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Binding globulin rises, not falls; a fall would lower total thyroxine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin is not linked to thyroid hormone clearance in the lecture.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A physiology study tracks healthy women from conception onward and records serial cardiovascular and renal measurements. The investigators aim to identify the primary initial change that sets off the other hemodynamic adaptations of pregnancy, including changes in blood volume, cardiac function, and renal function. Which of the following changes is this initiating event?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An early fall in systemic vascular resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: An early rise in myocardial contractile force

choices.label: C
choices.text: An early rise in renal sodium and water retention

choices.label: D
choices.text: An early rise in resting maternal heart rate

choices.label: E
choices.text: An early rise in total red blood cell mass

explanation.summary: The decrease in systemic vascular resistance is the primary initial driver of pregnancy's cardiovascular changes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early in pregnancy, progesterone, estradiol, and relaxin cause systemic vasodilation, lowering SVR. The resulting 'underfilling' of the vascular tree prompts the kidneys to retain water and solutes, expanding plasma volume, and it is the stimulus for the subsequent changes in blood volume, cardiac function, and renal function.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Increased cardiac output follows increased blood volume and decreased afterload; it is not the trigger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal sodium and water retention is a response to vascular underfilling caused by the fall in SVR.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heart rate rises as part of the cardiac output response, downstream of the fall in SVR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Red cell mass rises later, in response to hemodilution-stimulated erythropoietin.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation is lying flat on her back for a growth ultrasound. After several minutes she becomes lightheaded and nauseated, and her blood pressure falls to 86/50 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Give supplemental oxygen and keep her supine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Proceed with urgent cesarean delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raise the head of the bed while supine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start an intravenous vasopressor infusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Turn her onto her left side

explanation.summary: Supine hypotensive syndrome is relieved by moving to the left lateral decubitus position.
explanation.whyCorrect: After about 20 weeks, the gravid uterus can compress the inferior vena cava and aorta when the patient lies supine, reducing venous return and cardiac output (supine hypotensive or aortocaval compression syndrome). Repositioning to the left lateral decubitus position restores blood flow and relieves symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Remaining supine perpetuates compression of the vena cava and aorta.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This positional problem resolves with repositioning and does not require delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She remains supine, so the uterus continues to compress the great vessels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vasopressors do not address the mechanical caval compression; repositioning does.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has an arterial blood gas drawn during an evaluation for a minor injury; she has no respiratory complaints. The results show a pH of 7.44, a decreased PaCO2, and a mildly decreased serum bicarbonate. Her respiratory rate is 14/min, the same as before pregnancy. Which of the following best accounts for her low PaCO2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A diaphragm-driven rise in breathing frequency

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fall in carbon dioxide output by maternal tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: A primary renal loss of filtered bicarbonate

choices.label: D
choices.text: A progesterone-driven rise in tidal volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: An estrogen-driven rise in breathing frequency

explanation.summary: Progesterone raises tidal volume (about 40%) and minute ventilation without changing respiratory rate, lowering CO2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Minute volume increases in pregnancy even though the respiratory rate is unchanged, because tidal volume rises by about 40%, largely driven by progesterone. The extra ventilation lowers blood CO2 and alkalinizes the blood; the kidneys compensate by excreting bicarbonate, but pH still rises to about 7.44, a respiratory alkalosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The respiratory rate does not change in pregnancy, as her unchanged rate confirms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The low PaCO2 reflects increased ventilation, not reduced CO2 production.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The low bicarbonate is renal compensation for the respiratory alkalosis, not the primary event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory rate stays the same; the increase in ventilation comes from tidal volume.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation has an abdominal ultrasound for an unrelated reason. Both kidneys measure about 1.5 cm longer than on imaging taken before pregnancy, and the renal collecting systems appear mildly dilated. She has no flank pain, fever, or urinary symptoms, and her urinalysis is normal. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute ascending pyelonephritis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bilateral renal artery stenosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Early autosomal polycystic kidney disease

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal adaptation to higher renal flow

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obstructing stone in the left ureter

explanation.summary: In pregnancy, kidneys grow 1-2 cm and the collecting system dilates as renal blood flow and GFR rise.
explanation.whyCorrect: Renal blood flow rises 50%-85% and GFR rises 40%-60% in pregnancy. To adjust, the kidneys enlarge (from 10-13 cm by 1-2 cm in length) and the collecting system dilates. In an asymptomatic patient with a normal urinalysis these findings are physiologic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: She has no fever, flank pain, or urinary abnormalities to suggest infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Renal blood flow increases in pregnancy; nothing suggests arterial narrowing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Physiologic enlargement of pregnancy explains the findings without invoking cystic disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She has no flank pain, and bilateral mild dilation with renal enlargement fits normal adaptation.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation presents with 3 days of nausea, vomiting, and malaise. She is jaundiced. Laboratory studies show a serum glucose of 48 mg/dL, elevated aminotransferases, and a prolonged prothrombin time. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin ursodeoxycholic acid with weekly fetal testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Give intravenous fluids and antiemetics, then discharge

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform appendectomy after surgical consultation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stabilize her and expedite delivery of the fetus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start a proton pump inhibitor and reassess in 1 week

explanation.summary: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy is a third-trimester obstetric emergency treated by prompt delivery.
explanation.whyCorrect: GI symptoms in the third trimester accompanied by jaundice, hypoglycemia, elevated liver enzymes, and coagulopathy suggest acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Unlike hyperemesis gravidarum or appendicitis, AFLP can rapidly progress to maternal liver failure, fetal compromise, and death if prompt delivery is delayed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ursodeoxycholic acid is used for intrahepatic cholestasis, which causes itching without liver failure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Supportive care alone treats uncomplicated vomiting; it delays the delivery AFLP requires.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Jaundice, hypoglycemia, and coagulopathy point to liver dysfunction, not appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acid suppression addresses reflux, not a life-threatening liver emergency.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation reports 2 weeks of intense itching that is worst on her palms and the soles of her feet. Examination shows excoriations but no primary skin lesions. Her fasting total bile acid level is elevated. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication to reduce her laboratory abnormality and her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oral antihistamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral folic acid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Proton pump inhibitor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Topical corticosteroid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid

explanation.summary: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy is treated with ursodeoxycholic acid plus close fetal monitoring.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pruritus without rash, especially of the palms and soles, with elevated fasting bile acids in the second or third trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. Ursodeoxycholic acid reduces bile acid levels and symptoms; management also includes close fetal monitoring and typically planned delivery at 36-37 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An antihistamine does not lower the bile acids that drive the itching and fetal risk.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Folic acid supplementation does not address impaired hepatic bile flow.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Acid suppression treats reflux and has no role in cholestasis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: There is no rash to treat; the problem is impaired hepatic bile flow.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation presents with 2 days of swelling, pain, warmth, and redness of her left calf only. Compression ultrasound confirms a deep vein thrombosis. Which of the following physiologic changes of pregnancy most directly contributes to her hypercoagulable state?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster venous return from lower vascular resistance

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher fibrinogen and factor VIII with less fibrinolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lower fibrinogen levels with heightened fibrinolysis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mild thrombocytosis from increased platelet production

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced plasma volume that raises blood viscosity

explanation.summary: Pregnancy is prothrombotic: clotting factors rise and fibrinolysis falls, raising venous thromboembolism risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy increases fibrinogen and factors VII, VIII, and X and reduces fibrinolytic activity. Together with slowed venous return from uterine compression of the pelvic veins and IVC, this creates a hypercoagulable state that protects against postpartum hemorrhage but increases the risk of DVT and pulmonary embolism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Uterine compression slows, rather than speeds, venous return from the legs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fibrinogen rises and fibrinolysis falls in pregnancy, the reverse of this option.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mild thrombocytopenia, not thrombocytosis, is common in pregnancy from platelet consumption.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma volume increases in pregnancy; it does not fall.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation has a routine prenatal visit. Her pulse is 90/min, and her blood pressure is lower than it was before pregnancy. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft systolic ejection murmur; she has no dyspnea, chest pain, or exercise limitation. Which of the following most likely accounts for the murmur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased circulating blood volume

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased stroke volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leaflet damage from prior endocarditis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Narrowing of the aortic valve orifice

explanation.summary: A physiologic systolic ejection murmur in pregnancy reflects increased stroke volume.
explanation.whyCorrect: Stroke volume rises in pregnancy in response to the increased blood volume and the marked fall in SVR (reduced afterload). The greater flow across the outflow tract produces a physiologic systolic ejection murmur, alongside the expected lower blood pressure and faster heart rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood volume rises 40%-50% in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SVR falls in pregnancy, which is why her blood pressure is lower.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nothing in her history suggests valvular damage; the murmur is physiologic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An asymptomatic patient with the expected vital-sign changes fits a flow murmur, not stenosis.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation undergoes metabolic testing as part of a research protocol. Compared with her prepregnancy values, her postprandial glucose is higher despite higher insulin levels, and her circulating free fatty acids are increased. Which of the following hormonal effects best explains both findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Estrogen reducing insulin resistance and fat breakdown

choices.label: B
choices.text: Placental lactogen raising insulin resistance and lipolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progesterone raising insulin sensitivity and fat storage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prolactin raising glycogen storage and fat storage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxin reducing insulin release and lipolysis

explanation.summary: Placental lactogen raises insulin resistance and lipolysis, sparing glucose for the fetus and supplying fatty acids to the mother.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human placental lactogen increases maternal insulin resistance, so glucose remains higher after meals and is prioritized for the fetus, and it increases lipolysis, providing fatty acids as an alternative maternal energy source.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin resistance increases in pregnancy, and fat breakdown is increased.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin sensitivity falls in pregnancy, and fat breakdown, not storage, explains the fatty acids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolactin prepares the breast for lactation; it does not explain insulin resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin acts on vasculature and pelvic ligaments; lipolysis is increased, not reduced.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A researcher compares breast tissue from a nulliparous adult woman with tissue from a woman in mid-pregnancy. The lactiferous duct system is present in both, but the milk-producing sacs are extensively developed only in the pregnant woman. Which of the following hormone pairs induces the growth of these structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldosterone and oxytocin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxytocin and estradiol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placental lactogen and relaxin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progesterone and prolactin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxin and cortisol

explanation.summary: Alveologenesis occurs only in pregnancy and is induced by progesterone and prolactin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lactiferous ducts develop throughout puberty, but alveoli, the small sacs that produce and store milk, develop only during pregnancy. Their growth is induced by progesterone and prolactin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone governs sodium retention, not breast alveolar growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Oxytocin is not described as inducing alveolar growth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placental lactogen and relaxin are not described as driving alveolar development.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin and cortisol are not the hormones that induce alveologenesis.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of breast alveolar cells obtained at about 18 weeks' gestation shows that cellular proliferation has stopped and that the cells now contain abundant rough endoplasmic reticulum and increased Golgi complexes. Which of the following best describes the process occurring at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Active milk secretion triggered by oxytocin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ductal branching driven mainly by estradiol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fibrofatty replacement of glandular breast tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Involution of alveoli under rising progesterone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory differentiation driven by prolactin

explanation.summary: Around 18 weeks, alveolar proliferation ceases and prolactin drives differentiation into secretory epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: At about the midpoint of pregnancy, alveolar proliferation stops and the tissue differentiates into a true secretory epithelium under the influence of prolactin. The acini gain Golgi complexes and rough endoplasmic reticulum in preparation for milk production, which remains blocked by progesterone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Milk production is still blocked by progesterone at this stage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ducts develop during puberty; the change here is alveolar secretory differentiation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glandular tissue is maturing for lactation, not being replaced.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Progesterone blocks milk production but does not cause the alveoli to involute.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman at 7 weeks' gestation reports that her breasts have begun to feel fuller and larger. The estradiol and progesterone that drive this initial breast enlargement are produced chiefly by which of the following structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenal cortex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior pituitary gland

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal adrenal gland

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypothalamic nuclei

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ovarian corpus luteum

explanation.summary: Early breast enlargement (from 6-8 weeks) is driven by corpus luteum estradiol and progesterone plus pituitary prolactin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mammary changes begin at 6-8 weeks of pregnancy. The initial increase in size and volume is driven by estradiol and progesterone made in the ovarian corpus luteum, together with prolactin from the anterior pituitary.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal cortex is not named as the source of these early sex steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The anterior pituitary contributes prolactin, not the estradiol and progesterone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fetal adrenal is not described as the source of early breast-stimulating hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hypothalamus does not secrete estradiol or progesterone.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation is enrolled in a study of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis in healthy pregnancy. Compared with her nonpregnant baseline, which of the following sets of hormone changes would be expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cortisol decreased, aldosterone decreased, prolactin increased

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol decreased, aldosterone increased, prolactin decreased

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cortisol increased, aldosterone decreased, prolactin decreased

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cortisol increased, aldosterone increased, prolactin increased

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cortisol unchanged, aldosterone unchanged, prolactin increased

explanation.summary: The HPA axis is upregulated in pregnancy, raising cortisol, aldosterone, and prolactin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy upregulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, resulting in increased cortisol, aldosterone, and prolactin levels. These adaptations support fetal growth and prepare the mother for childbirth and lactation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortisol and aldosterone rise rather than fall.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol and prolactin both rise in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Aldosterone and prolactin both rise in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cortisol and aldosterone increase; they are not unchanged.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 24 weeks' gestation presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting. Serum lipase is markedly elevated. She does not drink alcohol and takes only a prenatal vitamin. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause of her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adverse reaction to a prenatal vitamin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gallstones from estrogen-altered bile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypertriglyceridemia from placental lactogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pancreatic duct injury from uterine pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral infection of the pancreas

explanation.summary: Gallstones, promoted by estrogen's effects on biliary physiology, are the leading cause of acute pancreatitis in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy-associated hormonal changes, particularly increased estrogen, alter biliary physiology and increase gallstone formation. As a result, gallstones are the leading cause of acute pancreatitis in pregnancy, which presents with severe epigastric pain, nausea, and vomiting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing in her history implicates a medication; gallstones are the leading cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placental lactogen increases lipolysis, but gallstones are the leading cause of pregnancy pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Uterine compression is not described as a cause of pancreatitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral pancreatitis is not the leading cause in pregnancy; gallstones are.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with long-standing hypothyroidism stopped taking her levothyroxine when she learned she was pregnant, fearing harm to the fetus. She is now 9 weeks' gestation. Which of the following fetal risks is most directly related to her untreated condition at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal goiter from placental thyroxine overproduction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal hypoglycemia from reduced placental lactogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal macrosomia from excess thyroid hormone transfer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired fetal brain and nervous system development

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neonatal hyperthyroidism from maternal antibodies

explanation.summary: The fetus depends on maternal thyroid hormone in the first half of pregnancy for normal neurodevelopment.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the first half of pregnancy, the fetus relies on maternal thyroid hormone for normal brain and nervous system development. Untreated maternal hypothyroidism is associated with impaired fetal neurodevelopment as well as miscarriage, preeclampsia, and postpartum hemorrhage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The placenta is not described as producing thyroxine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Placental lactogen is unrelated to the consequences of maternal hypothyroidism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Untreated hypothyroidism means too little, not too much, thyroid hormone reaches the fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Maternal hypothyroidism is not linked to neonatal hyperthyroidism in the lecture.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A physiology course tracks serial measurements in a healthy pregnant volunteer. By the time her total blood volume peaks, it has risen by nearly half, while her red blood cell mass has risen more modestly. At about what gestational age does the rise in blood volume peak, and by roughly how much has red cell mass increased?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peak at 12-16 weeks; red cell mass up about 50%

choices.label: B
choices.text: Peak at 20-24 weeks; red cell mass up about 40%

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peak at 28-32 weeks; red cell mass up about 20%

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peak at 28-32 weeks; red cell mass up about 50%

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peak at 36-40 weeks; red cell mass up about 5%

explanation.summary: Blood volume rises 40%-50%, peaking at 28-32 weeks, while red cell mass rises about 20%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Increases in blood volume begin very early and peak at 28-32 weeks, reaching 40%-50% above baseline. Red blood cell mass increases by approximately 20%. Because plasma expands more than red cells, the hematocrit remains 15%-20% below nonpregnant values.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The peak occurs at 28-32 weeks, and red cell mass rises about 20%, not 50%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The peak is later, and a 40% red cell rise would nearly match plasma, removing the dilutional anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The timing is right, but a 50% red cell rise would match blood volume and prevent physiologic anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The peak is at 28-32 weeks, and red cell mass rises more than 5%.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 20 weeks' gestation has a hemoglobin level lower than expected for her stage of pregnancy, and her physician suspects the decrease is not explained by hemodilution alone. Which of the following is the most common pathologic cause of anemia in pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune hemolysis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta-thalassemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Folate deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Iron deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sickle cell disease

explanation.summary: Iron deficiency is the most common pathologic cause of anemia in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: When evaluating anemia in pregnancy, first decide whether the fall in hemoglobin reflects normal hemodilution or a pathologic process. Iron deficiency is the most common pathologic cause; inherited hemoglobinopathies should also be considered in selected patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune hemolysis is not the most common pathologic cause of anemia in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thalassemia is considered with a personal or family history but is not the most common cause.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron deficiency, not folate deficiency, is named as the most common pathologic cause.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sickle cell disease should be considered, especially with a relevant history, but is less common than iron deficiency.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation presents for her first prenatal visit. She reports that her brother has lifelong anemia and has needed blood transfusions, and that she herself was told she had 'abnormal blood' as a child. Her hemoglobin is below the expected range for pregnancy. In addition to evaluating for iron deficiency, which of the following should be included in her workup?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compression ultrasound of both legs

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fasting glucose tolerance testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemoglobinopathy screening

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum bile acid measurement

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroid-binding globulin level

explanation.summary: Hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease and thalassemia should be screened for, especially with a personal or family history.
explanation.whyCorrect: Beyond iron deficiency, inherited hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease and thalassemia should be considered, particularly in patients with a personal or family history of anemia or abnormal hemoglobin screening. Screening is an important component of prenatal care because these conditions affect both maternal and fetal outcomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leg ultrasound evaluates deep vein thrombosis, not anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucose testing does not address an inherited red cell disorder.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bile acids are measured for suspected intrahepatic cholestasis, not anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid-binding globulin does not help evaluate a familial anemia.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 27 weeks' gestation has a routine complete blood count. She is asymptomatic, and her pregnancy is uncomplicated. The white blood cell count is mildly elevated with a neutrophil predominance, and the platelet count is mildly decreased. Which of the following is the best interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow suppression by placental lactogen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dilutional drop in all cell lines from plasma expansion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Early bacterial infection with consumptive thrombocytopenia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expected changes of pregnancy, including gestational thrombocytopenia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Primary myeloproliferative disorder unmasked by pregnancy

explanation.summary: Pregnancy normally raises the white count (mainly neutrophils) and causes mild thrombocytopenia from increased platelet consumption.
explanation.whyCorrect: In addition to the increase in blood volume, pregnancy increases the white blood cell count, particularly neutrophils. A mild thrombocytopenia is common because of increased platelet consumption. In an asymptomatic patient these findings are physiologic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Marrow suppression would not raise the neutrophil count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The white count rises rather than falls, so dilution alone cannot explain the pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She is asymptomatic, and both findings are expected in normal pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mild neutrophilia with mild thrombocytopenia is the normal pattern of pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation reports aching pain in her lower back that worsens by the end of the day. On examination she has an exaggerated inward curvature of the lower spine and no neurologic deficits. Which of the following best explains this postural change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Compensation for a forward shift in center of gravity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased ligament laxity at the sacroiliac joints

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of vertebral bone mass from calcium transfer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Muscle spasm from reduced abdominal wall pressure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nerve root compression by the descending fetal head

explanation.summary: Lumbar lordosis compensates for the forward shift in center of gravity and contributes to low back pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: As the enlarging uterus and breasts shift the center of gravity forward, lumbar lordosis develops to maintain balance. Although a normal compensation, it contributes to low back pain, which affects more than 50% of pregnant persons, especially in the second and third trimesters.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Ligament laxity increases, not decreases, in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bone loss is not the mechanism described for pregnancy lordosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Intra-abdominal pressure rises, not falls, in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She has no neurologic deficits, and lordosis is a postural compensation.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman who had a resting heart rate of 70/min before pregnancy is followed with serial echocardiograms. Which of the following best describes the expected course of her cardiac output and heart rate during pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Output peaks during the first trimester at 30%-50% below baseline; rate about 90/min

choices.label: B
choices.text: Output peaks in the first trimester at 10%-20% above baseline; rate about 70/min

choices.label: C
choices.text: Output peaks in the second trimester at 80%-100% above baseline; rate about 110/min

choices.label: D
choices.text: Output peaks in the third trimester at 10%-15% above baseline; rate about 60/min

choices.label: E
choices.text: Output peaks in the third trimester at 30%-50% above baseline; rate about 90/min

explanation.summary: Cardiac output peaks in the third trimester at about 30%-50% above baseline, and heart rate rises from about 70 to about 90/min.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cardiac output increases in response to pregnancy hormones and increased blood volume, through both higher stroke volume and higher heart rate, peaking in the third trimester at about 30%-50% above baseline. Heart rate rises from about 70/min before pregnancy to about 90/min.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiac output rises in pregnancy; it does not fall.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Output keeps rising into the third trimester, and heart rate increases.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both the magnitude of the output rise and the heart rate are overstated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The output rise is understated, and heart rate increases rather than falls.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with known moderate mitral stenosis is at 30 weeks' gestation. Before pregnancy she had no limitations, but she now reports worsening dyspnea, and bibasilar crackles are heard on examination. Which of the following best explains her decompensation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased heart rate prolonging diastolic filling

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher blood volume and output across a fixed valve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance raising afterload

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced tidal volume causing hypoventilation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxin-induced softening of the mitral valve leaflets

explanation.summary: Rising blood volume and cardiac output in pregnancy can decompensate stenotic valve disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The substantial increases in maternal blood volume and cardiac output stress the cardiovascular system and can worsen preexisting heart disease. Patients with stenotic valve lesions are at particular risk for dyspnea, pulmonary edema, arrhythmias, and decompensation as pregnancy progresses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heart rate increases in pregnancy, to about 90/min.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SVR falls in pregnancy, decreasing afterload.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tidal volume increases by about 40% in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin is not described as acting on heart valves.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has her blood pressure recorded at each prenatal visit throughout an uncomplicated pregnancy. Which of the following best describes the expected trend in her mean arterial pressure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Falls in the first trimester, then stays flat

choices.label: B
choices.text: Falls until about 30 weeks, then rises toward labor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rises steadily from conception until delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rises until about 20 weeks, then falls in labor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stays constant throughout, then falls in labor

explanation.summary: Mean arterial pressure falls gradually through about 30 weeks and then rises before and during labor.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood pressure reflects blood volume and cardiac output (both increased) and SVR (decreased). Normal MAP varies with gestational age: it decreases gradually but steadily through about 30 weeks and then increases prior to and during labor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MAP keeps falling until about 30 weeks and then rises.
whyWrongByChoice.C: MAP falls, rather than rises, through the first ~30 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the true pattern of an early fall and a late rise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MAP is not constant; it falls through about 30 weeks.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with chronic hypertension that is well controlled on enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide has a positive home pregnancy test, confirmed in the office at 6 weeks' gestation. Which of the following changes to her current regimen is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continue both enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Discontinue both enalapril and hydrochlorothiazide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Discontinue enalapril but continue hydrochlorothiazide

choices.label: D
choices.text: Discontinue hydrochlorothiazide but continue enalapril

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increase the enalapril dose and stop hydrochlorothiazide

explanation.summary: ACE inhibitors are teratogenic and thiazide diuretics should also be avoided in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Certain preferred antihypertensives are contraindicated in pregnancy because of fetal effects. ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are teratogens and should be avoided, and thiazide diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide or chlorthalidone should also be avoided, so both of her current agents need to be stopped.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both of these agents should be avoided in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Thiazide diuretics should also be avoided in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enalapril is a teratogen and must not be continued.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Increasing a teratogenic ACE inhibitor is inappropriate.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation has a chest x-ray to evaluate a mild cough. She is afebrile and has clear lungs on auscultation. The radiologist notes an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Which of the following additional features of the silhouette would be expected as a normal effect of pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Globular with a water-bottle contour

choices.label: B
choices.text: Narrowed and shifted to the right

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal in size but shifted downward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obscured by a widened mediastinum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shifted to the left

explanation.summary: In pregnancy, the cardiac silhouette is enlarged and shifted to the left.
explanation.whyCorrect: Along with increased tidal volume and a slightly increased chest diameter, the cardiac silhouette on frontal and lateral chest x-rays is enlarged and shifted to the left. The heart itself can enlarge by up to 12% to maintain blood flow to mother and fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A water-bottle contour is not the described physiologic change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The silhouette is enlarged and shifted left, not narrowed and shifted right.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The silhouette is enlarged, not normal in size, and it shifts left.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A widened mediastinum is not a described physiologic change of pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: Two women at 20 weeks' gestation have similar serum relaxin levels. One has severe pelvic and joint instability, while the other has no musculoskeletal symptoms. Which of the following statements about relaxin and joint laxity best accounts for this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Relaxin acts only on the uterus, so joint symptoms have another cause

choices.label: B
choices.text: Relaxin causes laxity in proportion to its level, so one woman misreported

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relaxin peaks at term, so symptoms at 20 weeks are unrelated to it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxin softens pelvic ligaments, but other factors shape laxity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Relaxin tightens the sacroiliac joints, so symptoms reflect its absence

explanation.summary: Relaxin softens the pelvic girdle ligaments, but generalized joint laxity varies with genetics, neuromuscular control, and biomechanics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Relaxin peaks in the first trimester, remains elevated, and has a well-established role in softening the pelvic girdle ligaments, especially the sacroiliac joints and pubic symphysis. Its effects on generalized joint laxity are variable; genetic predisposition, neuromuscular control, and biomechanical adaptations also contribute, which explains why some pregnant persons develop instability while others with similar hormone profiles do not.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Relaxin acts on the pelvic girdle ligaments, not only the uterus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Laxity is not simply proportional to relaxin level; other factors contribute.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Relaxin peaks in the first trimester and stays elevated throughout pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin softens, rather than tightens, the sacroiliac joints and pubic symphysis.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation reports numbness and tingling in the thumb, index, and middle fingers of both hands, worse at night. Her ankles are also swollen. Which of the following best describes the cause and expected course of her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical disk herniation from lumbar lordosis; needs surgery in pregnancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fluid retention compressing the median nerve; improves after delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron deficiency causing peripheral neuropathy; improves with iron alone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Relaxin-induced wrist laxity stretching the ulnar nerve; lasts for years

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombosis of hand veins from hypercoagulability; needs anticoagulation

explanation.summary: Pregnancy carpal tunnel syndrome results from fluid retention compressing the median nerve and improves after delivery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Carpal tunnel syndrome is common in pregnancy, especially in the third trimester. Fluid retention swells the carpal tunnel and compresses the median nerve, causing numbness, tingling, pain, and weakness in the thumb, index, middle, and lateral ring finger. Symptoms are often bilateral and improve after delivery as edema resolves; physical therapy is recommended as needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cause is edema in the carpal tunnel, and physical therapy is the recommended treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The lecture ties these symptoms to median nerve compression, not iron deficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The distribution fits the median nerve, and symptoms resolve after delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The finger distribution reflects median nerve compression, not venous thrombosis.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation reports a burning sensation behind her sternum and regurgitation of food when she lies flat after meals. Which of the following combinations of changes best explains her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faster gastric emptying and a tighter lower esophageal sphincter

choices.label: B
choices.text: Faster gastric emptying and lower intra-abdominal pressure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Normal gastric emptying and lower intra-abdominal pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Slower gastric emptying and a looser lower esophageal sphincter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Slower gastric emptying and a tighter lower esophageal sphincter

explanation.summary: Reflux in pregnancy results from slower gastric emptying, a relaxed lower esophageal sphincter, and raised intra-abdominal pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: During pregnancy food leaves the stomach more slowly, increasing the chance it moves back into the esophagus. GI smooth muscle relaxation also relaxes the lower esophageal sphincter, and the growing fetus raises intra-abdominal pressure; together these produce acid reflux, heartburn, and regurgitation when supine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric emptying slows and the sphincter relaxes in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Emptying slows and intra-abdominal pressure rises in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Emptying slows and intra-abdominal pressure increases in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes rather than tightens.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation presents with 1 day of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Her white blood cell count is elevated. Her physician is concerned about appendicitis but notes that diagnosis in pregnancy is difficult. Which of the following best explains this difficulty?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Appendicitis causes jaundice and hypoglycemia that mimic fatty liver

choices.label: B
choices.text: Appendicitis occurs only in the first trimester, so late cases are overlooked

choices.label: C
choices.text: Relaxin blunts peritoneal pain fibers, so pain is usually absent

choices.label: D
choices.text: The appendix is pushed inferiorly and leukocytosis is rare in pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: The appendix shifts superiorly and GI symptoms and leukocytosis mimic pregnancy

explanation.summary: In pregnancy the enlarging uterus shifts the appendix superiorly, and nausea, vomiting, and leukocytosis can mimic normal pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Appendicitis can occur at any stage of pregnancy. Diagnosis is difficult because the enlarging uterus can shift the appendix superiorly, altering the location of pain, and because nausea, vomiting, and leukocytosis may mimic normal pregnancy changes such as the physiologic rise in neutrophils.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Jaundice and hypoglycemia point to acute fatty liver of pregnancy, not appendicitis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Appendicitis can occur at any stage of pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Relaxin is not described as affecting abdominal pain perception.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The appendix shifts superiorly, and leukocytosis is a normal finding in pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has had vomiting many times each day for 2 weeks and cannot keep down fluids. She has lost 4 kg. She has dry mucous membranes, her urine is positive for ketones, and her serum electrolytes are abnormal. Her liver enzymes and bilirubin are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute appendicitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gallstone pancreatitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperemesis gravidarum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Hyperemesis gravidarum is first-trimester severe vomiting with dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, ketonuria, and weight loss.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hyperemesis gravidarum most commonly occurs in the first trimester and is characterized by severe, persistent vomiting leading to dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, ketonuria, and weight loss. It goes well beyond ordinary morning sickness, which is common in early pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing here suggests appendicitis; the picture is prolonged vomiting with volume depletion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: AFLP typically occurs in the third trimester with jaundice, hypoglycemia, and coagulopathy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pancreatitis presents with severe epigastric pain, which is not described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ICP occurs later in pregnancy and presents with pruritus of the palms and soles.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman who delivered 3 months ago reports that large amounts of hair are coming out in her brush and in the shower. During pregnancy she noticed her hair became unusually thick. Her scalp examination shows diffuse thinning without scarring or inflammation. Which of the following best explains her hair loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Androgen excess from persistent placental hormones

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune scarring of the scalp triggered by delivery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pemphigoid gestationis involving the scalp

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postpartum iron deficiency destroying hair follicles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Telogen shedding after a prolonged pregnancy anagen phase

explanation.summary: Prolonged anagen in pregnancy thickens hair, followed by postpartum telogen effluvium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some individuals experience hair thickening during pregnancy because the anagen (growth) phase is prolonged. After delivery, this is followed by telogen effluvium, a diffuse shedding of hair.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Androgen excess is not described as a postpartum hair change.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no scarring or inflammation; the shedding is diffuse and nonscarring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pemphigoid gestationis is a pregnancy dermatosis, not a cause of diffuse postpartum shedding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lecture links the shedding to the hair cycle, not to iron deficiency.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation has been diagnosed with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy and started on appropriate medication. Her most recent fasting total bile acid level is 118 micromol/L. Which of the following fetal complications is of greatest concern, and what delivery plan is typically recommended?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal anemia; immediate delivery at diagnosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Macrosomia; await labor until 41 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neural tube defects; delivery at 40 weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stillbirth; await spontaneous labor to 42 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stillbirth; planned delivery at 36-37 weeks

explanation.summary: In ICP, fetal risk (especially stillbirth) rises with bile acids >100 micromol/L, and planned delivery at 36-37 weeks is typical.
explanation.whyCorrect: ICP is associated with preterm labor, meconium-stained amniotic fluid, and stillbirth, particularly when bile acid levels exceed 100 micromol/L. Management includes close fetal monitoring, ursodeoxycholic acid, and typically planned delivery at 36-37 weeks to reduce the risk of fetal demise.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fetal anemia is not a described ICP risk; delivery is typically planned at 36-37 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Macrosomia is not a described ICP risk, and waiting to 41 weeks raises stillbirth risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neural tube defects are not associated with ICP, and delivery is planned earlier.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stillbirth is the concern, which is why delivery is not delayed to 42 weeks.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with cirrhosis and known esophageal varices becomes pregnant. Her hepatologist warns that pregnancy may increase her risk of variceal hemorrhage. Which of the following physiologic changes of pregnancy most directly underlies this concern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased clotting factor levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased heart rate and stroke volume

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decreased renal blood flow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased blood volume and cardiac output

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased systemic vascular resistance

explanation.summary: Rising blood volume and cardiac output in pregnancy can worsen portal hypertension in cirrhosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy substantially increases maternal blood volume and cardiac output, which can worsen portal hypertension in patients with cirrhosis. These patients face higher risks of esophageal variceal hemorrhage, ascites, coagulopathy, and hepatic decompensation, as well as fetal risks such as growth restriction, preterm birth, and stillbirth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clotting factors rise, not fall, in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heart rate and stroke volume both increase in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Renal blood flow increases 50%-85% in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Systemic vascular resistance falls in pregnancy.

questions.topicName: Pregnancy Effects on Other Organ Systems

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus after glucose tolerance testing. She had normal glucose levels before pregnancy. She asks why her blood sugar is now high. Which of the following best describes the underlying mechanism of her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells triggered by placental antigens

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excess maternal cortisol suppressing glucose uptake by skeletal muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal insulin crossing the placenta and down-regulating maternal receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased renal glucose reabsorption raising the maternal glucose set point

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin resistance not matched by an adequate rise in insulin secretion

explanation.summary: GDM results from pregnancy-related insulin resistance that the maternal pancreas fails to compensate for with increased insulin secretion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin resistance rises steadily through the second and third trimesters, so more insulin is needed to maintain euglycemia. A normal pancreas increases secretion to keep up; when the maternal insulin response is inadequate, maternal and then fetal hyperglycemia develop. GDM therefore reflects both insulin resistance and inadequate insulin secretion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune beta-cell destruction describes type 1 (insulin-deficient) diabetes, not the insulin-resistance mechanism of GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lecture attributes pregnancy insulin resistance to placental hormones such as hPL, not to a cortisol excess.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The fetus makes its own insulin in response to maternal glucose; fetal insulin is not the cause of maternal hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GDM is not caused by renal glucose handling; glucosuria is actually normal in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation has rising postprandial glucose values and increased circulating free fatty acids compared with her first trimester. Which of the following hormones is primarily responsible for these changes, which help direct maternal glucose toward the fetus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corpus luteum progesterone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human chorionic gonadotropin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human placental lactogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal pituitary prolactin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ovarian relaxin

explanation.summary: Human placental lactogen (hPL) increases maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis, directing glucose to the fetus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy hormones rise steadily through the second and third trimesters and increase tissue insulin resistance. hPL is the hormone the lecture names as mediating this resistance and the accompanying increase in lipolysis, so postprandial glucose rises and glucose not taken up by maternal cells is used by the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corpus luteum progesterone is not the hormone that mediates late-pregnancy insulin resistance and lipolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: hCG is not the hormone that mediates the insulin resistance and lipolysis of late pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolactin is not identified as the mediator of pregnancy insulin resistance and lipolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Relaxin is not involved in pregnancy glucose metabolism in this way.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes for her first prenatal visit at 10 weeks' gestation. She asks whether anything in her history raises her chance of developing gestational diabetes mellitus. Which of the following features of her history is a risk factor for this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Body mass index of 23 kg/m2 before pregnancy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia treated during adolescence

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polycystic ovarian syndrome diagnosed at age 19

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prior son weighing 7 lb 2 oz at birth

choices.label: E
choices.text: Seasonal allergic rhinitis treated with antihistamines

explanation.summary: A history of PCOS is a listed risk factor for GDM.
explanation.whyCorrect: Risk factors for GDM include age 25 or older, certain races/ethnicities, obesity (BMI >30), excessive gestational weight gain, prior glucose intolerance, history of PCOS, prior GDM, prior infant over 9 lb, multiple gestation, and family history of diabetes. Of the options, only her PCOS is on that list.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A BMI of 23 is not obese; obesity as a risk factor means BMI >30.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Iron-deficiency anemia is not a risk factor for GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A prior infant counts as a risk factor only if large (>9 lb); 7 lb 2 oz is not.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allergic rhinitis has no association with GDM.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has gestational diabetes mellitus that has been poorly controlled because she has not followed her dietary plan. She asks which problem is most likely to result. Which of the following is the most common complication of her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal macrosomia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neonatal hypocalcemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polyhydramnios

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preeclampsia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Umbilical cord prolapse

explanation.summary: Fetal macrosomia is the most common complication of GDM.
explanation.whyCorrect: High maternal glucose reaches the fetus, which is effectively overfed and grows larger than it should in utero. This fetal macrosomia (a large-for-gestational-age infant) is the most common complication of GDM and underlies the delivery complications such as shoulder dystocia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neonatal hypocalcemia is a recognized newborn risk but not the most common complication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polyhydramnios occurs in GDM but is less common than macrosomia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preeclampsia is a major maternal complication of GDM, but not the most common complication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cord prolapse is a downstream complication of polyhydramnios, not the most common GDM complication.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation with gestational diabetes mellitus has fingerstick glucose values well above target. Ultrasound shows a markedly increased amniotic fluid volume and an accelerated fetal growth curve. Which of the following best explains the increase in amniotic fluid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal hyperglycemia producing increased fetal urine output

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal glycosuria increasing the osmolality of the amniotic fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placental overproduction of amniotic fluid stimulated by human placental lactogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reduced fetal swallowing from esophageal compression by the enlarged uterus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transudation of fluid across chorionic membranes from maternal hyperglycemia

explanation.summary: In GDM, fetal hyperglycemia causes fetal polyuria, and because amniotic fluid is largely fetal urine, polyhydramnios results.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal and fetal glucose levels are the same, so maternal hyperglycemia exposes the fetus to high glucose. The fetus develops increased urination (polyuria), and since amniotic fluid is basically fetal urine, this manifests as polyhydramnios. Fetal hyperinsulinemia also increases fat deposition, explaining the accelerated growth.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal urine does not contribute to amniotic fluid; the source is fetal urine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: hPL mediates maternal insulin resistance and lipolysis; it does not produce amniotic fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lecture explains polyhydramnios in GDM by increased fetal urine production, not reduced swallowing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Excess fluid in GDM comes from fetal urine, not transudation across membranes.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus delivers a 10-lb 4-oz boy vaginally. Delivery is prolonged because the anterior shoulder becomes impacted behind the pubic symphysis. After birth, the infant's right arm hangs limply at his side and he does not move the shoulder or elbow, but his right hand grasp is strong. Which of the following structures was most likely injured?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical spinal cord at the C3-C4 level

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lower trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Right phrenic nerve in the neck

choices.label: D
choices.text: Right radial nerve at the spiral groove

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6)

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia in a macrosomic infant can stretch the upper brachial plexus, causing Erb palsy (C5-C6).
explanation.whyCorrect: Macrosomic infants are at risk for shoulder dystocia because the shoulders are the widest part of the body. Trauma to the shoulders and upper arms can cause brachial plexus injuries such as Erb palsy, a C5-C6 injury that weakens the shoulder and elbow while the hand is spared, as in this infant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A cervical cord injury would produce bilateral and more widespread deficits, not a single limp arm.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A lower-trunk (C8-T1) injury would affect the hand; his grasp is strong.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Phrenic nerve injury affects the diaphragm and breathing, not arm movement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radial nerve injury at the spiral groove causes wrist drop, not loss of shoulder and elbow movement.

questions.stem: A term boy is born by cesarean delivery to a 34-year-old woman whose gestational diabetes mellitus was poorly controlled. Two hours after birth, he is jittery, and his serum glucose is 30 mg/dL. Which of the following best explains his low glucose level?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deficient hepatic glycogen stores from chronic placental insufficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal hyperinsulinemia persisting after the umbilical cord is clamped

choices.label: C
choices.text: Impaired gluconeogenesis from liver immaturity related to prematurity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neonatal adrenal insufficiency from intrauterine glucocorticoid exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfer of maternal insulin across the placenta just before delivery

explanation.summary: Fetuses of hyperglycemic mothers increase their own insulin production, which predisposes the newborn to hypoglycemia once the maternal glucose supply ends at birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal and fetal glucose levels are equal, so a fetus exposed to high glucose increases its own insulin production. After delivery, the maternal glucose supply is cut off, but the newborn's elevated insulin output persists, producing hypoglycemia, which is a listed postnatal risk for infants of mothers with GDM.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Placental insufficiency is not described in GDM; these fetuses are overfed and often macrosomic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This infant is term, so prematurity-related liver immaturity does not apply.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Adrenal insufficiency is not a described complication of GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lecture describes the fetus producing its own excess insulin in response to glucose; maternal insulin transfer is not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 25 weeks' gestation drinks a 50-g glucose solution, and her blood glucose 1 hour later is 158 mg/dL. She has no symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Check a urine dipstick for glucose at each visit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes and begin insulin therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obtain a hemoglobin A1c level to confirm the diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perform a fasting 3-hour test with a 100-g load

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat the same 50-g screen in 4 weeks

explanation.summary: A 1-hour 50-g screen of 140 mg/dL or greater is followed by a fasting 3-hour 100-g glucose tolerance test.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 1-hour 50-g glucose screen is only a screening test. A result of 140 or greater fails the screen, and the patient proceeds to a fasting 3-hour test: a fasting glucose is drawn, she drinks 100 g of glucose, and glucose is drawn at 1, 2 and 3 hours and compared with predefined cutoffs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Urine glucose is not useful because glucosuria is normal in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A failed screen does not establish the diagnosis; confirmatory testing is needed, and lifestyle change, not insulin, is first-line.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin A1c is not yet part of most official GDM diagnostic criteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A failed screen should be followed by confirmatory testing, not a repeat screen.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 27 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus after a confirmatory glucose tolerance test. She has not yet received any treatment. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin twice-weekly nonstress tests now

choices.label: B
choices.text: Diet modification and regular exercise

choices.label: C
choices.text: Schedule induction of labor at 37 weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start basal insulin at bedtime

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start metformin with meals

explanation.summary: First-line treatment of GDM is lifestyle modification: regular exercise and a structured diet.
explanation.whyCorrect: With confirmed GDM, the first-line treatment is regular exercise and a diet of 1800-2500 calories per day (40% carbohydrate, 40% fat, 20% protein). Most patients can manage GDM this way; medication is added only if glucose targets are not met.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antenatal fetal testing is done in the third trimester, not as the initial treatment at diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Early induction is not part of the initial management described for GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin is used only if targets are not met despite diet and exercise.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Metformin is reserved for when lifestyle change fails and has less safety evidence than insulin.

questions.stem: Five women with gestational diabetes mellitus have followed diet and exercise for 2 weeks. Their typical fingerstick glucose values are listed below. Which patient's values indicate that pharmacologic therapy should now be added?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fasting 90 mg/dL; 2 hours after meals 115 mg/dL

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fasting 92 mg/dL; 2 hours after meals 118 mg/dL

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fasting 93 mg/dL; 1 hour after meals 148 mg/dL

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fasting 94 mg/dL; 1 hour after meals 136 mg/dL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fasting 95 mg/dL; 2 hours after meals 120 mg/dL

explanation.summary: Medication is started when, despite lifestyle change, fasting glucose is >95 mg/dL, 2-hour postprandial >120 mg/dL, or 1-hour postprandial >140 mg/dL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thresholds for adding medication are fasting fingerstick glucose >95 mg/dL, 2-hour postprandial >120 mg/dL, or 1-hour postprandial >140 mg/dL. Only the 1-hour postprandial value of 148 mg/dL exceeds a threshold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Both values are within target.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fasting 92 and 2-hour 118 are both at or below the thresholds (>95 and >120).
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 1-hour value of 136 is below the >140 threshold, and fasting 94 is not above 95.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These values equal but do not exceed the thresholds; medication is started when fasting is >95 or 2-hour is >120.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus controlled by diet delivers a healthy infant. She asks whether she needs any further glucose evaluation now that the baby is born. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Check glucose levels 24-72 hours after delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue the pregnancy diet plan for the next 6 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recheck the 50-g glucose screen at her 6-week visit only

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start metformin to prevent future type 2 diabetes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop all glucose testing because the condition resolves

explanation.summary: Glucose is checked 24-72 hours postpartum to determine whether the patient actually has type 2 diabetes mistakenly diagnosed as GDM.
explanation.whyCorrect: GDM normally resolves shortly after delivery, and the patient can return to a normal diet. Glucose concentrations should still be checked 24-72 hours postpartum to distinguish hyperglycemia that was solely a product of pregnancy from type 2 diabetes misdiagnosed as GDM; persistent elevation requires diabetes treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Once GDM resolves, the patient can return to a normal diet.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 50-g screen is a pregnancy screening test; the lecture calls for glucose checks 24-72 hours postpartum.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Medication is not started prophylactically; treatment is needed only if glucose remains elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although GDM usually resolves, postpartum glucose testing is still needed to detect underlying type 2 diabetes.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation has gestational diabetes mellitus with persistently elevated fasting glucose despite treatment. Her physician plans antenatal testing because poor control raises the risk of intrauterine fetal demise. Which of the following surveillance regimens is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daily contraction stress tests until delivery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monthly maternal hemoglobin A1c measurement only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nonstress tests once or twice each week

choices.label: D
choices.text: Weekly amniocentesis for fetal lung maturity

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weekly maternal serum placental lactogen levels

explanation.summary: Third-trimester fetal surveillance in GDM includes nonstress tests one to two times weekly plus ultrasound.
explanation.whyCorrect: Poorly controlled GDM increases the risk of intrauterine fetal demise, so antenatal tests of fetal well-being are done in the third trimester. These include nonstress tests one to two times per week, which assess fetal heart rate patterns over time, and ultrasounds to assess well-being and amniotic fluid volume.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Daily contraction stress tests are not the described regimen; nonstress tests are used.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hemoglobin A1c does not assess the fetus and is not the monitoring tool described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serial amniocentesis is not part of the fetal surveillance described for GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.E: hPL levels are not used to monitor fetal well-being.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman who has had type 1 diabetes since age 12 learns that she is 6 weeks pregnant. Which of the following terms best classifies her diabetes in this pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gestational diabetes mellitus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Impaired glucose tolerance of pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physiologic glucosuria of pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pregestational diabetes

explanation.summary: Diabetes present before conception is pregestational diabetes; GDM is diabetes that develops during pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: GDM is the development of diabetes mellitus in a pregnant patient. It is contrasted with pregestational diabetes, in which a female who already has diabetes becomes pregnant, which describes this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GDM refers to diabetes that develops during pregnancy; hers predates the pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Her diabetes is long-standing type 1 disease, not a pregnancy-related glucose intolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: She has type 1 diabetes, not a monogenic diabetes syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Glucosuria can be normal in pregnancy, but she has established diabetes.

questions.stem: A healthy 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation reports that she is hungrier than usual and feels full for a long time after meals. Which of the following metabolic changes is expected at this stage of pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Accelerated gastric emptying after meals

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased insulin secretion with higher glucose

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased insulin secretion promoting fat storage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased lipolysis with rising fasting glucose

choices.label: E
choices.text: Marked insulin resistance driven by high hPL

explanation.summary: In the first half of pregnancy, increased insulin secretion lowers glucose and promotes maternal fat deposition.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the first half of pregnancy, rising pregnancy hormones lead to lower glucose levels, maternal fat deposition, delayed gastric emptying and increased appetite. Increased pancreatic insulin secretion lets the body use glucose efficiently and store the excess as fat.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gastric emptying is delayed, not accelerated, in the first half of pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin secretion increases early in pregnancy, lowering glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased lipolysis belongs to later pregnancy, and glucose is lower, not higher, early on.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin resistance develops as pregnancy progresses into the second and third trimesters.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has normal glucose tolerance. Compared with her nonpregnant state, which of the following best describes her pancreatic insulin secretion at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased by about 25%

choices.label: B
choices.text: Essentially unchanged

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased by about 10%

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased by about 300%

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased by about 50%-100%

explanation.summary: To overcome third-trimester insulin resistance, insulin secretion rises up to 50%-100% above nonpregnant levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pregnancy hormones increase steadily through the second and third trimesters, raising tissue insulin resistance. More insulin is required to maintain euglycemia, and insulin secretion increases progressively, up to 50%-100% in the third trimester compared with the nonpregnant state.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin secretion rises, not falls, in normal late pregnancy.
