whyWrongByChoice.B: Secretion must increase to overcome rising insulin resistance.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 10% rise understates the increase described for the third trimester.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A 300% rise overstates the 50%-100% increase described.

questions.stem: A healthy 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation with a normal glucose screen checks her glucose out of curiosity and finds that her overnight and between-meal values are lower than they were before pregnancy. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Continuous fetal uptake of glucose crossing the placenta

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased maternal lipolysis during overnight fasting

choices.label: C
choices.text: Down-regulation of hepatic glucagon receptors in pregnancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased maternal insulin sensitivity caused by hPL

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of hepatic glucose output by progesterone

explanation.summary: In pregnancies with a normal insulin response, the fetus continuously consumes maternal glucose, causing relative maternal hypoglycemia between meals and during sleep.
explanation.whyCorrect: Despite relative insulin resistance, pregnant patients with a normal pancreatic insulin response become hypoglycemic between meals and while sleeping compared with their nonpregnant state. This happens because the fetus continues to use glucose that crosses the placenta from the maternal circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lipolysis increases, not decreases, as pregnancy progresses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Glucagon receptor changes are not the explanation given for maternal fasting hypoglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: hPL increases insulin resistance, not insulin sensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lecture attributes this finding to fetal glucose consumption, not progesterone effects on the liver.

questions.stem: A healthy 29-year-old woman is now at 32 weeks' gestation. Compared with the metabolic state in her first trimester, which of the following changes is expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased pancreatic insulin secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Faster maternal glucose uptake into muscle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greater deposition of new maternal fat

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased breakdown of maternal fat stores

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lower glucose levels after meals

explanation.summary: As insulin resistance develops in later pregnancy, lipolysis increases and postprandial glucose rises.
explanation.whyCorrect: As pregnancy progresses, the pregnant person becomes insulin resistant. She is less able to use glucose, so postprandial glucose rises and lipolysis (breakdown of fat) increases. Glucose not readily taken up by her cells is used by the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insulin secretion rises progressively through late pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insulin resistance makes maternal cells less able to take up glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fat deposition is a first-half feature; later pregnancy favors lipolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Postprandial glucose rises, not falls, as insulin resistance develops.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman at 16 weeks' gestation asks how common gestational diabetes mellitus is in the United States. Which of the following is the best estimate of its prevalence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1 of every 100 pregnancies

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 6-8 of every 100 pregnancies

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 15-20 of every 100 pregnancies

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 25-30 of every 100 pregnancies

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 40-50 of every 100 pregnancies

explanation.summary: GDM affects about 6%-8% of US pregnancies, roughly 7 of every 100.
explanation.whyCorrect: The prevalence of GDM in the United States is fairly high at 6%-8%, with approximately 7 of 100 pregnant patients developing the condition.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 1% underestimates the 6%-8% prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 15%-20% overestimates the prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 25%-30% greatly overestimates the prevalence.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 40%-50% greatly overestimates the prevalence.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 2, comes for her first prenatal visit. She is concerned about gestational diabetes. Which of the following additional findings in her obstetric history would most increase her risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prior daughter weighing 7 lb 6 oz

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prior son weighing 8 lb 2 oz

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prior son weighing 9 lb 10 oz

choices.label: D
choices.text: An uncomplicated prior vaginal delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Postpartum depression after her first birth

explanation.summary: Previous birth of a large infant (>9 lb) is a risk factor for GDM.
explanation.whyCorrect: Listed risk factors for GDM include previous birth of a large infant weighing more than 9 lb. A prior son of 9 lb 10 oz meets this threshold; the other birth weights do not.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 7-lb 6-oz infant is not large and does not meet the >9-lb threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An 8-lb 2-oz infant is below the >9-lb threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An uncomplicated prior vaginal delivery is not a risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Postpartum depression is not a listed risk factor for GDM.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus has had normal blood pressure at every visit. At 34 weeks' gestation, her blood pressure is 152/98 mm Hg and urinalysis shows 2+ protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic hypertension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Placental abruption

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polyhydramnios

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preeclampsia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pregestational diabetes

explanation.summary: Preeclampsia, new hypertension with proteinuria usually after 20 weeks, is a major maternal complication of GDM.
explanation.whyCorrect: A major maternal complication of GDM is preeclampsia: the development of hypertension and protein in the urine, usually after 20 weeks. Untreated hypertension can be catastrophic, including maternal and fetal death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Her blood pressure was normal at earlier visits, so this is new hypertension, not chronic hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Placental abruption is a complication of polyhydramnios and does not present as hypertension with proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Polyhydramnios is excess amniotic fluid, not hypertension with proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her diabetes developed in pregnancy, and diabetes type does not explain new hypertension with proteinuria.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with poorly controlled gestational diabetes mellitus has a fundal height 4 cm greater than expected for dates. At 36 weeks, her membranes rupture with a large gush of fluid. The fetal heart rate abruptly falls to 70/min, and a pulsatile structure is felt at the cervical os. Which of the following most likely predisposed her to this complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal growth restriction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal preeclampsia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oligohydramnios

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placenta previa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polyhydramnios

explanation.summary: Polyhydramnios in GDM predisposes to umbilical cord prolapse.
explanation.whyCorrect: GDM causes fetal polyuria and therefore polyhydramnios, which here is suggested by the large fundal height and the large gush of fluid. Complications of polyhydramnios include fetal malposition, placental abruption, preterm contractions, premature rupture of membranes, uterine atony and umbilical cord prolapse, which this vignette describes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GDM causes accelerated rather than restricted fetal growth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Preeclampsia is a GDM complication but does not predispose to cord prolapse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oligohydramnios is too little fluid; GDM causes excess fluid, and a large gush argues against it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Placenta previa is not the described predisposing factor for cord prolapse in GDM.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus at 31 weeks' gestation undergoes ultrasound, which shows polyhydramnios. Which of the following complications is she at increased risk of developing as a direct result of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal growth restriction

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal pulmonary hypoplasia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Placenta accreta

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placental abruption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Postterm pregnancy

explanation.summary: Polyhydramnios increases the risk of placental abruption, among other complications.
explanation.whyCorrect: Possible complications of polyhydramnios include fetal malposition, maternal respiratory compromise, placental abruption, preterm contractions and possibly preterm labor, premature rupture of membranes, uterine atony, and umbilical cord prolapse.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Growth restriction is not a complication of polyhydramnios; GDM fetuses tend to overgrow.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pulmonary hypoplasia is associated with too little amniotic fluid, not too much.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Placenta accreta is not listed as a complication of polyhydramnios.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polyhydramnios is associated with preterm contractions and labor, not postterm pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus is at 39 weeks' gestation. An ultrasound suggests that the fetus is macrosomic. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Await spontaneous labor until 42 weeks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Offer a cesarean delivery to avoid birth injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: Plan an operative vaginal delivery with forceps

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the 3-hour glucose tolerance test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start insulin to reduce fetal size before labor

explanation.summary: If term ultrasound suggests macrosomia, cesarean delivery may be offered to avoid shoulder dystocia and other birth injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Large-for-gestational-age infants are at risk of shoulder dystocia and other injury during vaginal delivery and may need cesarean delivery for fetal-pelvic disproportion. If an ultrasound at term suggests fetal macrosomia, a cesarean delivery may be offered.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Delaying delivery would allow further growth and does not reduce birth injury risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A forceps delivery does not avoid the shoulder dystocia risk of a macrosomic fetus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The diagnosis is already established; retesting does not address delivery risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Starting insulin at term will not shrink an already macrosomic fetus.

questions.stem: A 9-lb 12-oz girl is delivered vaginally to a mother with gestational diabetes mellitus after a delivery complicated by shoulder dystocia. On examination, there is swelling, crepitus and a bony step-off along the upper left chest wall between the sternum and shoulder. She cries when the left arm is moved but has a normal grasp. Which of the following injuries is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clavicle fracture

choices.label: B
choices.text: First rib fracture

choices.label: C
choices.text: Proximal humerus fracture

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scalp cephalohematoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upper brachial plexus stretch injury

explanation.summary: Shoulder dystocia in LGA infants can cause clavicle fracture as well as brachial plexus injury.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the shoulders are the widest part of the baby and can become stuck, shoulder dystocia can traumatize the shoulders and upper arms, leading to brachial plexus injuries and clavicle fracture. Crepitus and a step-off between the sternum and shoulder localize the injury to the clavicle.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A first rib fracture would not produce a palpable step-off along this line.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The findings lie between the sternum and shoulder, not in the upper arm.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A cephalohematoma involves the scalp, not the upper chest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A brachial plexus injury causes weakness, not crepitus and a palpable bony step-off.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation has gestational diabetes mellitus and has not been checking her glucose. Which of the following findings at this visit is most consistent with poor glycemic control affecting the fetus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fetal heart rate of 145/min on Doppler

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fundal height 4 cm less than expected for dates

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fundal height 5 cm greater than expected for dates

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trace bilateral ankle edema late in the day

choices.label: E
choices.text: Weight gain of about 1 lb over the past week

explanation.summary: Fetal macrosomia and polyhydramnios from poor control can make fundal height measure greater than expected for gestational age.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the fetus is exposed to high glucose, its insulin production increases, raising fat deposition and urine production. The resulting macrosomia and polyhydramnios are seen on ultrasound and can be detected as a fundal height greater than expected for gestational age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A fetal heart rate of 145/min is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A smaller-than-expected fundal height does not fit the overgrowth and excess fluid of poorly controlled GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mild dependent edema late in the day is not a sign of fetal effects of hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This finding does not indicate a fetal effect of hyperglycemia.

questions.stem: A term boy born to a mother with poorly controlled gestational diabetes mellitus had a hematocrit of 68% on the first day of life. At 48 hours, he is visibly jaundiced with an elevated indirect bilirubin. Mother and infant are both blood type O positive, and the direct antiglobulin test is negative. Which of the following best explains his jaundice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A factor in breast milk inhibiting bilirubin conjugation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic injury from neonatal hypocalcemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased breakdown of an elevated red cell mass

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal antibodies against fetal red cell antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Obstruction of the extrahepatic bile ducts

explanation.summary: Infants of mothers with GDM are at risk for polycythemia and hyperbilirubinemia from high red blood cell breakdown.
explanation.whyCorrect: After delivery, infants of mothers with GDM are at increased risk for hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, respiratory distress syndrome, polycythemia and hyperbilirubinemia. The hyperbilirubinemia results from high red blood cell breakdown, fitting this polycythemic infant with indirect hyperbilirubinemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Breast-milk jaundice appears later and does not explain the link to polycythemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypocalcemia is a separate neonatal risk and does not cause jaundice.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Same blood types and a negative direct antiglobulin test argue against immune hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bile duct obstruction causes direct (conjugated) hyperbilirubinemia, not an elevated indirect bilirubin at 48 hours.

questions.stem: A term girl is born to a mother whose gestational diabetes mellitus was poorly controlled throughout the third trimester. The pediatric team plans laboratory monitoring in the first day of life. Besides glucose, which of the following laboratory abnormalities is this newborn at increased risk of developing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypercalcemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperglycemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypernatremia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypocalcemia

explanation.summary: Newborns of mothers with GDM are at increased risk for hypocalcemia, along with hypoglycemia and polycythemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: After delivery, infants of mothers with GDM are at higher risk for hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, respiratory distress syndrome, polycythemia and hyperbilirubinemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These infants are at risk for polycythemia, the opposite of anemia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The listed calcium abnormality is hypocalcemia, not hypercalcemia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These infants are at risk for hypoglycemia, not hyperglycemia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hypernatremia is not a listed complication.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus asks about risks to her baby's breathing after birth. Which of the following conditions is her newborn at increased risk of developing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cystic fibrosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pulmonary hypoplasia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory distress syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tracheoesophageal fistula

explanation.summary: Respiratory distress syndrome is among the postnatal risks for infants of mothers with GDM.
explanation.whyCorrect: After delivery, infants of mothers with GDM are at higher risk for hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, respiratory distress syndrome, polycythemia and hyperbilirubinemia. The fetus is also at risk for premature birth.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diaphragmatic hernia is a structural anomaly not linked to GDM here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cystic fibrosis is genetic and unrelated to maternal glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pulmonary hypoplasia is associated with too little amniotic fluid; GDM causes excess fluid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tracheoesophageal fistula is not a listed GDM complication.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation asks whether a hemoglobin A1c measurement could replace the glucose-drink testing she was offered for gestational diabetes mellitus. Which of the following statements about hemoglobin A1c in pregnancy is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is avoided because the blood draw endangers the fetus

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the preferred first-line screen for gestational diabetes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It may assist diagnosis but is not yet in most official criteria

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reflects only the fasting glucose from the prior night

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replaces the 3-hour test whenever the value is at least 5.7%

explanation.summary: Hemoglobin A1c is sometimes used to assist in GDM diagnosis but is not yet part of most official GDM criteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tests used to diagnose diabetes in nonpregnant patients, such as fasting glucose and hemoglobin A1c, are less useful in pregnancy. Hemoglobin A1c is sometimes used to assist in diagnosis but has not yet become part of most official GDM criteria; GDM is diagnosed with oral glucose tolerance testing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A routine blood draw poses no fetal risk; that is not why A1c is limited.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The first-line screen is the 1-hour 50-g glucose test, not hemoglobin A1c.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hemoglobin A1c reflects chronic hyperglycemia, not a single fasting value.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No A1c cutoff replaces the 3-hour glucose tolerance test in GDM diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 26 weeks' gestation with no GDM risk factors drinks a 50-g glucose solution. Her blood glucose 1 hour later is 136 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Begin a 1800-2500 calorie diet and exercise plan

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continue routine prenatal care, no further testing

choices.label: C
choices.text: Obtain a hemoglobin A1c to exclude the diagnosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perform a fasting 3-hour 100-g glucose tolerance test

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start fingerstick glucose checks four times daily

explanation.summary: A 1-hour 50-g screen below 140 mg/dL is a passed screen, so confirmatory testing is not needed.
explanation.whyCorrect: The patient fails the 1-hour 50-g screen only if the value is 140 or greater, in which case she proceeds to the 3-hour test. A value of 136 mg/dL is a passed screen, so routine care continues.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lifestyle therapy is for confirmed GDM, which she does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemoglobin A1c is not part of most official GDM criteria and is not needed after a passed screen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The 3-hour test follows only a failed screen (140 or greater).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fingerstick monitoring is for managing confirmed GDM.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with gestational diabetes mellitus at 28 weeks' gestation and meets with a dietitian to begin first-line therapy. Which of the following macronutrient distributions is recommended?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 20% carbohydrate, 40% fat, 40% protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: 30% carbohydrate, 50% fat, 20% protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: 40% carbohydrate, 40% fat, 20% protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: 50% carbohydrate, 30% fat, 20% protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: 60% carbohydrate, 20% fat, 20% protein

explanation.summary: The GDM diet is 1800-2500 calories per day, with 40% carbohydrate, 40% fat and 20% protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: First-line GDM treatment is regular exercise plus a diet of 1800-2500 calories per day, with 40% of calories from carbohydrates, 40% from fats and 20% from protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Protein is 20%, not 40%, and carbohydrate is 40%, not 20%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fat is 40%, not 50%, and carbohydrate is 40%, not 30%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 50% carbohydrate and 30% fat do not match the recommended 40/40/20 split.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 60% carbohydrate is higher than the recommended 40%.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman with newly confirmed gestational diabetes mellitus starts diet and exercise therapy. She is taught to check her glucose with a home meter to judge whether treatment is working. How often should she usually perform this testing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Four times daily

choices.label: B
choices.text: Once daily, fasting only

choices.label: C
choices.text: Once weekly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only at prenatal visits

choices.label: E
choices.text: Twice monthly

explanation.summary: Glucose testing, usually four times daily, is used to determine the effectiveness of GDM treatment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Frequent glucose testing, usually four times daily, is necessary to determine whether GDM treatment is effective, including whether fasting and postprandial targets are being met.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Fasting-only testing misses postprandial values, which also guide therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Weekly testing is too infrequent to judge treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testing only at visits cannot guide day-to-day management.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Twice-monthly testing is far less frequent than recommended.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus has had fasting fingerstick glucose values of 100-105 mg/dL despite 2 weeks of diet and exercise. Her physician decides to begin medication. Which of the following agents is most often used in this situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glyburide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metformin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pioglitazone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sitagliptin

explanation.summary: When lifestyle therapy fails in GDM, insulin is the agent most often used.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pharmacologic therapy is needed if fasting glucose exceeds 95 mg/dL despite diet and exercise, as here. Insulin is most often used; oral agents such as metformin are becoming more common but have less evidence of safety.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glyburide is not the agent most often used in GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metformin is increasingly used but has less safety evidence and is not the most commonly used agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pioglitazone is not described as a GDM treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sitagliptin is not described as a GDM treatment.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus requiring insulin is at 34 weeks' gestation. In addition to nonstress testing, her physician orders a third-trimester ultrasound as part of antenatal surveillance. Which of the following does this ultrasound primarily assess?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cervical length and funneling pattern

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fetal karyotype and chromosome count

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal lung maturity and surfactant level

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fetal well-being and amniotic fluid volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Placental hormone and hPL output

explanation.summary: Third-trimester ultrasound in GDM assesses fetal well-being and the amount of amniotic fluid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because poorly controlled GDM increases the risk of intrauterine fetal demise, antenatal tests are done in the third trimester: nonstress tests one to two times weekly and ultrasounds to assess fetal well-being and amniotic fluid volume. Ultrasound can also show macrosomia and polyhydramnios.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cervical length is not the purpose of GDM surveillance ultrasound.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Karyotype requires genetic testing, not ultrasound.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ultrasound does not measure fetal lung maturity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ultrasound cannot measure placental hormone production.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman had gestational diabetes mellitus 2 years ago. Her glucose returned to normal after delivery, and she is not pregnant now. She asks whether that pregnancy has any lasting implications for her health. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Certain progression to diabetes within 5 years

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated lifetime risk of type 1 diabetes mellitus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Need for lifelong metformin to prevent diabetes

choices.label: E
choices.text: No greater diabetes risk than the general population

explanation.summary: Patients with GDM, even when it resolves, have an increased risk of type 2 diabetes later in life.
explanation.whyCorrect: GDM normally resolves shortly after delivery, but patients who develop GDM, even if it resolves after pregnancy, are at increased risk of developing type 2 diabetes mellitus later in life.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Risk is increased, but progression is not certain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The increased later risk is for type 2, not type 1, diabetes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Treatment is needed only if glucose remains elevated; lifelong metformin is not indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A history of GDM raises later diabetes risk above that of the general population.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with gestational diabetes mellitus has had fasting glucose values above target for weeks. Ultrasound at 34 weeks shows an accelerated fetal growth curve with increased fetal subcutaneous fat. Which of the following best explains the fetal overgrowth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Excess growth hormone secretion by the fetal pituitary gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human placental lactogen acting directly on fetal fat cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased fetal insulin output driven by high glucose exposure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal insulin crossing the placenta and stimulating fetal tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced fetal glucose uptake causing compensatory fat storage

explanation.summary: Because fetal glucose mirrors maternal glucose, maternal hyperglycemia raises fetal insulin production, which increases fat deposition and growth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maternal and fetal serum glucose levels are the same. When the fetus is exposed to high glucose, its own insulin production increases, which increases fat deposition (and urine production). The fetus is effectively overfed and grows more than it should, producing macrosomia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fetal growth hormone excess is not the mechanism described for macrosomia in GDM.
whyWrongByChoice.B: hPL acts on maternal metabolism (insulin resistance and lipolysis), not directly on fetal fat.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lecture describes the fetus increasing its own insulin output, not maternal insulin driving growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fetal glucose uptake is increased, not reduced, in GDM.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes for her first prenatal visit at 13 weeks' gestation. She has not seen a physician in several years. Her blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg and, 4 hours later, 146/92 mm Hg. Urinalysis shows no protein. She has no headache, visual changes, or abdominal pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic hypertension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eclampsia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gestational hypertension

choices.label: D
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preeclampsia

explanation.summary: Hypertension found before 20 weeks' gestation is classified as chronic hypertension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic hypertension is high blood pressure that is preexisting or found before 20 weeks' gestation. Her readings exceed 140/90 mm Hg at 13 weeks, so the elevation is presumed to have preceded the pregnancy. Gestational hypertension and its related disorders develop only after 20 weeks.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Eclampsia is preeclampsia complicated by seizures; she has had no seizure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gestational hypertension is new-onset hypertension that develops only after 20 weeks' gestation; she is at 13 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HELLP syndrome requires hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets; nothing suggests these.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Preeclampsia is diagnosed beyond 20 weeks and requires proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; she has neither and is at 13 weeks.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old primigravida at 30 weeks' gestation has a blood pressure of 144/92 mm Hg, confirmed at 146/94 mm Hg 5 hours later. At 16 weeks her blood pressure was 112/70 mm Hg. She has no headache or visual changes. Urine protein is negative, and platelet count, creatinine, and liver enzymes are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Close maternal and fetal monitoring without drug therapy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immediate induction of labor at 30 weeks' gestation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Magnesium sulfate infusion for seizure prophylaxis today

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral hydrochlorothiazide to reduce plasma volume now

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral labetalol titrated to keep pressure below 140/90 mm Hg

explanation.summary: Gestational hypertension below the severe range is monitored closely; drugs are reserved for pressures above 160/110 mm Hg.
explanation.whyCorrect: She has gestational hypertension: new hypertension after 20 weeks with no proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. Pharmacotherapy is generally reserved for severe hypertension (>160/110 mm Hg), so the correct approach is close monitoring of mother and fetus while watching for signs of preeclampsia, eclampsia, or HELLP syndrome.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Gestational hypertension without preeclampsia does not call for delivery at 30 weeks; it is monitored.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Magnesium sulfate is given for preeclampsia with severe features or eclampsia; she has neither proteinuria nor severe features.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thiazide diuretics are among the drugs that are dangerous in pregnancy, and drug therapy is not yet indicated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Labetalol is pregnancy-safe, but in gestational hypertension medication is reserved for severe-range pressures above 160/110 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 29 weeks' gestation with gestational hypertension has a blood pressure of 168/112 mm Hg, confirmed on repeat measurement 15 minutes later. Prompt treatment to lower her blood pressure is planned. Which of the following is the most appropriate medication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chlorthalidone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrochlorothiazide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Labetalol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lisinopril

choices.label: E
choices.text: Losartan

explanation.summary: Labetalol is one of the preferred antihypertensives in pregnancy; ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and thiazides are avoided.
explanation.whyCorrect: Severe hypertension (>=160/110 mm Hg) requires prompt treatment. The preferred agents in pregnancy are hydralazine, methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine ("Hypertensive Mothers Love Nifedipine"). ACE inhibitors/ARBs and thiazide diuretics are dangerous in pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chlorthalidone is a thiazide-type diuretic, a class to avoid in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic, a class to avoid in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor, a class that is dangerous in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Losartan is an ARB, a class that is dangerous in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old primigravida at 33 weeks' gestation has a blood pressure of 150/96 mm Hg and, 6 hours later, 152/98 mm Hg. Her blood pressure was 114/72 mm Hg at 12 weeks. A 24-hour urine collection contains 480 mg of protein. Platelet count, creatinine, and liver enzymes are normal. She has no headache, visual symptoms, or seizures. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic hypertension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eclampsia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gestational hypertension

choices.label: D
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preeclampsia

explanation.summary: New hypertension after 20 weeks on two readings at least 4 hours apart plus proteinuria >300 mg/24 h is preeclampsia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Preeclampsia is diagnosed beyond 20 weeks when blood pressure exceeds 140/90 mm Hg on two occasions at least 4 hours apart with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. More than 300 mg of protein in a 24-hour urine may indicate preeclampsia; she has 480 mg.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Her blood pressure was normal at 12 weeks, so the hypertension did not precede 20 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eclampsia requires new-onset seizures; she has had none.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gestational hypertension has no proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction; her 24-hour urine protein is 480 mg.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HELLP syndrome requires hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets; her labs are normal.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman delivers at 34 weeks' gestation because of preeclampsia. Histologic study of the placental bed is performed. Compared with the maternal vessels supplying a normal placenta, which of the following best describes the vessels feeding her intervillous space?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete endothelial replacement by maternal fibroblasts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excessively deep trophoblast invasion into the vessel wall

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased blood flow delivered into the intervillous space

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of smooth muscle producing wide low-resistance channels

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retained muscular media that remains vasoconstrictive

explanation.summary: Shallow cytotrophoblast invasion leaves spiral arteries unremodeled, with a responsive muscular wall that stays vasoconstrictive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Preeclampsia is associated with shallow cytotrophoblast invasion, which impairs spiral artery remodeling. The non-remodeled vessels keep an intact, responsive tunica media that remains vasoconstrictive, reducing blood flow to the intervillous space and causing placental oxidative stress and hypoxia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is not the lesion; the vessels are intact and non-remodeled with a responsive muscular wall.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The defect is shallow, not excessive, cytotrophoblast invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Flow to the intervillous space is reduced, not increased, leading to placental hypoxia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of the muscular wall is what normal remodeling achieves; in preeclampsia remodeling fails.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation with preeclampsia with severe features is started on magnesium sulfate. One hour later her blood pressure is 166/112 mm Hg and, 15 minutes after that, 164/110 mm Hg. She has not had a seizure, and her reflexes are present. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Add intravenous labetalol for blood pressure control

choices.label: B
choices.text: Add oral lisinopril for blood pressure control

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continue magnesium alone and recheck in 4 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase the magnesium dose until the pressure falls

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop magnesium because it failed to lower pressure

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate prevents seizures but does not lower blood pressure; severe hypertension needs a separate antihypertensive.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute severe hypertension (>=160/110 mm Hg) requires urgent treatment to reduce complications such as maternal stroke. Magnesium sulfate is given for seizure prophylaxis but is not an antihypertensive, so patients often need both magnesium and a pregnancy-safe blood pressure-lowering drug such as labetalol.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ACE inhibitors are dangerous in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Severe-range hypertension requires urgent treatment to reduce the risk of maternal stroke.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Magnesium sulfate is not an antihypertensive; raising the dose will not treat the hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Magnesium is given for seizure prophylaxis, not blood pressure, and should continue.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation is diagnosed with preeclampsia after blood pressures of 146/94 and 148/92 mm Hg taken 5 hours apart and a 24-hour urine protein of 400 mg. She has no headache, visual changes, or abdominal pain. Laboratory studies are normal, her pressure stays below 160/110 mm Hg, and fetal testing is reassuring. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Close monitoring with delivery at 37 weeks' gestation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delivery only after spontaneous onset of labor

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expectant management continued until 41 weeks' gestation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immediate cesarean delivery at 35 weeks' gestation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Magnesium sulfate with induction within 24 hours

explanation.summary: Preeclampsia without severe features is monitored closely and delivered at 37 weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delivery is the definitive treatment for preeclampsia, with timing based on gestational age and severe features. Without severe features, delivery is recommended at 37 weeks; before then, the patient and fetus are monitored closely.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Waiting for labor ignores the recommendation to deliver at 37 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delivery is recommended at 37 weeks, not continued pregnancy to 41 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immediate delivery is not indicated for stable preeclampsia without severe features before 37 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Without severe features she does not need urgent magnesium and delivery at 35 weeks.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation with a blood pressure of 162/108 mm Hg has a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in the labor triage unit. The seizure stops after 1 minute, her airway is protected, and she is placed on her side. Which of the following should be given to prevent further seizures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydralazine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Labetalol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Magnesium sulfate

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methyldopa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nifedipine

explanation.summary: Magnesium sulfate is the drug of choice to prevent recurrent seizures in eclampsia.
explanation.whyCorrect: A seizure in a pregnant patient with hypertension after 20 weeks is eclampsia. Management is to administer magnesium sulfate to prevent additional seizures, stabilize the patient, and then deliver regardless of gestational age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydralazine is an antihypertensive, not seizure prophylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Labetalol lowers blood pressure but does not prevent seizures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methyldopa is an antihypertensive, not seizure prophylaxis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nifedipine is an antihypertensive, not seizure prophylaxis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain, nausea, and vomiting. Her blood pressure is 154/100 mm Hg. Hemoglobin is 9.1 g/dL, platelet count is 68,000/mm3, AST is 310 U/L, and ALT is 280 U/L. A peripheral smear shows helmet-shaped and triangular red cell fragments. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eclampsia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gestational hypertension

choices.label: C
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placental abruption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preeclampsia without severe features

explanation.summary: Hemolysis with schistocytes, elevated transaminases, and thrombocytopenia define HELLP syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: HELLP syndrome is hemolysis (microangiopathic, with schistocytes), elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. Symptoms, when present, include right upper quadrant pain and tenderness, nausea, vomiting, and headache. It is considered a severe form of preeclampsia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eclampsia requires seizures; she has none.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gestational hypertension lacks end-organ dysfunction; she has hemolysis, liver injury, and low platelets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Abruption presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain, not schistocytes with elevated transaminases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Her hemolysis, transaminase elevation, and thrombocytopenia are far beyond this; they define HELLP.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation is found to have hemolysis with schistocytes, an AST of 290 U/L, and a platelet count of 72,000/mm3. Her blood pressure was 158/104 mm Hg and has been lowered with intravenous labetalol; magnesium sulfate is infusing. She has no active bleeding, and fetal heart rate tracing is reassuring. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Discharge home with twice-weekly laboratory checks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expectant management until 34 weeks' gestation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expectant management until 37 weeks' gestation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proceed with prompt delivery at 30 weeks' gestation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Prophylactic platelet transfusion and continued pregnancy

explanation.summary: HELLP syndrome is treated by stabilizing the patient and delivering promptly regardless of gestational age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delivery is the definitive treatment for any patient with HELLP syndrome. Once the mother is stabilized (antihypertensive, magnesium, blood products as indicated), delivery proceeds promptly regardless of gestational age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HELLP is an obstetric urgency; outpatient management is unsafe.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Delaying to 34 weeks is a consideration only in select stable preeclampsia; HELLP calls for prompt delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Waiting to 37 weeks applies to preeclampsia without severe features, not HELLP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Platelets are given for active bleeding, and continuing the pregnancy is not appropriate in HELLP.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, comes for a prenatal visit at 10 weeks' gestation. Her previous pregnancy ended in an uncomplicated term vaginal delivery. Her history includes mild intermittent asthma, iron-deficiency anemia treated last year, an appendectomy at age 15, and type 1 diabetes mellitus since age 12. Which of the following in her history most increases her risk for preeclampsia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Appendectomy at age 15

choices.label: B
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia treated last year

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mild intermittent asthma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prior uncomplicated term vaginal delivery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type 1 diabetes mellitus

explanation.summary: Preexisting medical conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, or kidney disease are risk factors for preeclampsia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Risk factors for preeclampsia include chronic hypertension, prior preeclampsia or pregnancy complications, family history, advanced maternal age, preexisting diabetes, hypertension, or kidney disease, first pregnancy, and multiple gestation. Her pregestational diabetes is the one listed risk factor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A remote appendectomy is not a preeclampsia risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Treated iron deficiency is not a preeclampsia risk factor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asthma is not among the risk factors for preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: First pregnancy is the risk factor; a prior uncomplicated pregnancy does not add risk.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation with HELLP syndrome begins oozing blood from her intravenous sites and gums. Prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time are prolonged, fibrinogen is low, D-dimer is markedly elevated, and platelet count is 32,000/mm3. Which of the following best explains her bleeding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies directed against factor VIII

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of clotting factors by systemic coagulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inherited deficiency of von Willebrand factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Isolated platelet destruction with normal clotting factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Magnesium sulfate blockade of platelet adhesion

explanation.summary: HELLP can cause DIC, in which widespread clotting consumes coagulation factors and causes profuse bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Disseminated intravascular coagulation is a serious complication of HELLP syndrome. Systemic activation of the coagulation cascade deposits clots throughout the body, causing ischemic organ damage, and consumes coagulation factors, causing profuse bleeding. Prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, and high D-dimer fit this picture.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An acquired factor VIII inhibitor would not explain low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, and thrombocytopenia in HELLP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An inherited defect would not newly cause low fibrinogen and prolonged PT with HELLP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Her prolonged PT/PTT and low fibrinogen show clotting factors are also depleted.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This is not the mechanism; the laboratory picture shows factor consumption.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has her blood pressure checked at each prenatal visit. Which of the following is the lowest blood pressure that meets the threshold for clinically significant hypertension in pregnancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 120/80 mm Hg

choices.label: B
choices.text: 130/80 mm Hg

choices.label: C
choices.text: 135/85 mm Hg

choices.label: D
choices.text: 140/90 mm Hg

explanation.summary: Clinically significant hypertension in pregnancy is >=140 systolic and/or >=90 diastolic, the same as in nonpregnant adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnostic thresholds in pregnancy are the same as in nonpregnant adults: systolic >=140 mm Hg and/or diastolic >=90 mm Hg. 160/110 mm Hg marks severe hypertension, which needs prompt treatment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 120/80 mm Hg is below the threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 130/80 mm Hg is below the pregnancy threshold of 140/90 mm Hg.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 135/85 mm Hg is below the threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 160/110 mm Hg is the severe-range threshold; the lower threshold for significant hypertension is 140/90 mm Hg.

questions.stem: A physician reviewing maternal mortality data notes that hypertensive disorders are the leading cause of maternal death in the United States but rank second worldwide. Which of the following is the leading cause of maternal death worldwide?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peripartum cardiomyopathy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pregnancy-associated bleeding

choices.label: C
choices.text: Puerperal sepsis after delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ruptured ectopic pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Venous thromboembolism

explanation.summary: Worldwide, hypertension is second only to pregnancy-associated bleeding as a cause of maternal death.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypertension is the second leading cause of maternal death worldwide, second only to pregnancy-associated bleeding. In the United States, hypertension is the leading cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cardiomyopathy is not the cause that outranks hypertension worldwide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sepsis is not the cause that outranks hypertension worldwide.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ectopic rupture is not the cause that outranks hypertension worldwide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thromboembolism is not the cause that outranks hypertension worldwide.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation who has missed several prenatal visits and has untreated high blood pressure comes to the emergency department with sudden vaginal bleeding and constant abdominal pain. Her uterus is tender. Her blood pressure is 158/100 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute kidney failure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eclampsia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gestational hypertension

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placental abruption

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary edema

explanation.summary: Placental abruption, a complication of untreated hypertension in pregnancy, presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain.
explanation.whyCorrect: In placental abruption, the placenta detaches from the uterus before delivery. It typically presents as vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain and carries a high risk of death for mother and baby, requiring stabilization and delivery. Untreated hypertension in pregnancy increases its risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Kidney failure does not present with vaginal bleeding and uterine tenderness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eclampsia is defined by seizures, not vaginal bleeding with abdominal pain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hypertension alone does not explain vaginal bleeding and a tender uterus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulmonary edema causes respiratory symptoms, not vaginal bleeding.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman with chronic hypertension learns she is 7 weeks pregnant. She asks which blood pressure medication must be avoided during pregnancy. Which of the following is it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hydralazine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hydrochlorothiazide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Labetalol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Methyldopa

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nifedipine

explanation.summary: Thiazide diuretics (and ACE inhibitors/ARBs) are dangerous in pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Many antihypertensives used in nonpregnant patients are dangerous in pregnancy, specifically ACE inhibitors/ARBs and thiazide diuretics. Hydralazine, methyldopa, labetalol, and nifedipine are preferred.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hydralazine is a preferred antihypertensive in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Labetalol is a preferred antihypertensive in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Methyldopa is a preferred antihypertensive in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nifedipine is a preferred antihypertensive in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation has a new blood pressure elevation to 146/94 mm Hg, confirmed 5 hours later; her pressure was normal at 11 weeks. Urine protein is negative. She asks why it matters that her high blood pressure began during pregnancy rather than before it. Which of the following is the most important reason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It makes ACE inhibitors safe for use in the third trimester

choices.label: B
choices.text: It mandates drug therapy once pressure reaches 140/90

choices.label: C
choices.text: It may signal preeclampsia, eclampsia, or HELLP syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires delivery as soon as it is diagnosed

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires magnesium sulfate for the rest of gestation

explanation.summary: Gestational hypertension is distinguished from chronic hypertension mainly because it may be caused by preeclampsia, eclampsia, or HELLP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The main reason to separate gestational from chronic hypertension is that gestational hypertension may be caused by one of the serious hypertensive disorders, so they must be sought. If they are absent, chronic and gestational hypertension are treated the same.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE inhibitors remain dangerous in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Medication in gestational hypertension is reserved for severe pressures above 160/110 mm Hg.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gestational hypertension without preeclampsia is monitored, not delivered at diagnosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Magnesium is for preeclampsia with severe features or eclampsia, not uncomplicated gestational hypertension.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation has new blood pressures of 148/96 and 150/94 mm Hg measured 5 hours apart. A 24-hour urine collection is sent. Which of the following results would support a diagnosis of preeclampsia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 60 mg of protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: 150 mg of protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: 220 mg of protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: 280 mg of protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: 410 mg of protein

explanation.summary: More than 300 mg of protein in a 24-hour urine collection may indicate preeclampsia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Proteinuria in preeclampsia is defined as more than 300 mg of protein in urine collected over 24 hours. Only 410 mg exceeds that threshold.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 60 mg is below the 300 mg threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 150 mg is below the 300 mg threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 220 mg is below the 300 mg threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 280 mg is below the 300 mg threshold.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation who has been normotensive throughout pregnancy has a blood pressure of 150/96 mm Hg at a routine visit. Urine dipstick shows 2+ protein. She is asymptomatic, and platelet count, creatinine, and liver enzymes are normal. Before a diagnosis of preeclampsia can be made, which of the following is required?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A blood pressure at or above 160/110 mm Hg

choices.label: B
choices.text: A second high reading at least 4 hours later

choices.label: C
choices.text: A witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated liver enzymes on repeat laboratory testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: New headache or visual scotomata on history

explanation.summary: Preeclampsia requires elevated blood pressure on two occasions measured at least 4 hours apart.
explanation.whyCorrect: Preeclampsia is diagnosed beyond 20 weeks when blood pressure exceeds 140/90 mm Hg on two separate occasions at least 4 hours apart, with proteinuria or end-organ dysfunction. A single reading is not enough.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Severe-range pressure is not required; 140/90 mm Hg suffices.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A seizure would indicate eclampsia; it is not required for preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Organ dysfunction is an alternative to proteinuria, not a requirement when proteinuria is present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Symptoms are not required; many patients with preeclampsia are asymptomatic.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with long-standing type 1 diabetes complicated by kidney involvement is at 31 weeks' gestation. Before conception, her 24-hour urine protein was 600 mg. Today her 24-hour urine protein is 700 mg. Her blood pressure has ranged from 118/74 to 126/80 mm Hg throughout pregnancy, including today. Platelet count and liver enzymes are normal. Which of the following best explains her proteinuria?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gestational hypertension

choices.label: B
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Preeclampsia without severe features

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preexisting diabetic nephropathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superimposed preeclampsia

explanation.summary: Proteinuria from preexisting diabetes or kidney disease can predate pregnancy; a careful history prevents misdiagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with diabetes or kidney disease may have proteinuria that predates pregnancy, and pregnancy can worsen it. Without new hypertension after 20 weeks, the preeclampsia criteria (and the other hypertensive disorders) are not met.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gestational hypertension requires elevated blood pressure, which she does not have.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HELLP requires hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets; her labs are normal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preeclampsia requires blood pressure above 140/90 mm Hg; hers is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superimposed preeclampsia occurs on chronic hypertension; she is normotensive.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation has new hypertension and a 24-hour urine protein of 900 mg. Which of the following best explains the proteinuria in her condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ascending bacterial infection of the renal pelvis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endothelial dysfunction altering glomerular blood flow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immune complex deposition in the basement membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overflow of light chains made by plasma cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tubular injury from nephrotoxic drug exposure

explanation.summary: Placental hypoxia releases factors causing endothelial dysfunction, which alters glomerular flow and produces proteinuria.
explanation.whyCorrect: In preeclampsia, placental hypoxia triggers release of molecules, reactive oxygen species, and cytokines that cause endothelial dysfunction, with inflammation, vasoconstriction, and decreased blood flow. One consequence is abnormal glomerular blood flow leading to proteinuria from small-vessel disease in the kidneys.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Infection is not the mechanism of preeclampsia proteinuria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preeclampsia proteinuria is attributed to endothelial dysfunction, not immune complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Overflow proteinuria is unrelated to preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Drug toxicity is not the mechanism described for preeclampsia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 31 weeks' gestation is admitted with preeclampsia with severe features after pressures up to 164/110 mm Hg. After intravenous labetalol and magnesium sulfate, her blood pressure is 148/96 mm Hg, her laboratory values are stable, and fetal testing is reassuring. She is at a center with maternal-fetal medicine and a neonatal intensive care unit. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Discharge home with weekly blood pressure checks

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inpatient expectant care with delivery at 34 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inpatient expectant care with delivery at 37 weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Outpatient expectant care with delivery at 37 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop magnesium and manage as gestational hypertension

explanation.summary: Before 34 weeks, expectant management of severe preeclampsia may be considered only in stable patients at a high-risk facility.
explanation.whyCorrect: For preeclampsia with severe features, delivery is generally recommended at 34 weeks or later after stabilization. Before 34 weeks, expectant management may be considered only in carefully selected, stable patients at a facility equipped for high-risk maternal and neonatal care; deterioration requires delivery at any gestational age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Expectant management with severe features requires a high-risk inpatient setting.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The 37-week target applies to preeclampsia without severe features.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Severe features are not managed as outpatients, and delivery is targeted at 34, not 37, weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She has preeclampsia with severe features, not gestational hypertension.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation has blood pressures of 166/114 and 168/112 mm Hg with a severe headache and 3+ proteinuria. She receives intravenous hydralazine and magnesium sulfate, and her blood pressure falls to 150/98 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Delivery now that she has been stabilized

choices.label: B
choices.text: Delivery only if a seizure occurs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expectant management until 37 weeks' gestation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expectant management until 39 weeks' gestation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stop magnesium and discharge her home

explanation.summary: Preeclampsia with severe features at or beyond 34 weeks is delivered after stabilization.
explanation.whyCorrect: For preeclampsia with severe features, delivery is generally recommended at 34 weeks or later once the patient has been stabilized. She is at 35 weeks and stabilized with antihypertensive therapy and magnesium.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Delivery should not wait for eclampsia to develop.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Waiting to 37 weeks applies to preeclampsia without severe features.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Prolonging pregnancy is inappropriate with severe features beyond 34 weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She needs seizure prophylaxis and delivery, not discharge.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman at 29 weeks' gestation with preeclampsia with severe features is being managed expectantly at a tertiary center. On hospital day 3, she develops a persistent headache despite treatment, her creatinine rises, and fetal testing becomes nonreassuring. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A second oral antihypertensive and observation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continued expectant care until 34 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delivery regardless of the early gestational age

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transfer to outpatient care with home monitoring

choices.label: E
choices.text: Twice-daily fetal testing without other change

explanation.summary: Maternal or fetal deterioration requires delivery regardless of gestational age.
explanation.whyCorrect: Expectant management before 34 weeks is allowed only in stable patients. Maternal or fetal deterioration, as here, requires delivery regardless of gestational age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Added drugs do not replace delivery once deterioration occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deterioration ends expectant management.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A deteriorating patient cannot be managed as an outpatient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: More testing does not address maternal and fetal deterioration.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 5 days after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery with a severe headache and blurred vision. She was normotensive throughout pregnancy. Her blood pressure is 168/112 mm Hg and, 15 minutes later, 166/110 mm Hg. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Magnesium sulfate alone to bring down her pressure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral hydrochlorothiazide and clinic review in 6 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassurance, since preeclampsia always ends with delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recheck blood pressure at her routine 6-week visit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urgent antihypertensive therapy plus magnesium sulfate

explanation.summary: Preeclampsia can first appear after delivery; severe postpartum hypertension needs urgent treatment, with magnesium for neurologic symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Preeclampsia may persist, worsen, or first appear after delivery. Severe postpartum hypertension requires urgent antihypertensive treatment, and magnesium sulfate may be indicated when severe features or neurologic symptoms, such as her headache and visual change, are present.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Magnesium is not an antihypertensive; severe hypertension needs separate treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Severe hypertension needs urgent treatment, not delayed follow-up.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preeclampsia can first appear postpartum and requires treatment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Delay risks complications such as stroke.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman at an estimated 38 weeks' gestation who has had no prenatal care is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. She has no history of epilepsy. Her blood pressure is 164/106 mm Hg. Urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronic hypertension

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eclampsia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gestational hypertension

choices.label: D
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Placental abruption

explanation.summary: Eclampsia is preeclampsia with new seizures; proteinuria is usually present but can be absent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Eclampsia usually occurs after 20 weeks, most often in the third trimester. Proteinuria is seen as in preeclampsia but can be absent in some patients, so a negative dipstick does not exclude the diagnosis in a hypertensive pregnant patient with a new seizure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypertension alone does not explain a new seizure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gestational hypertension does not include seizures; hypertension plus a new seizure is eclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No hemolysis, liver enzyme, or platelet abnormalities are reported, and HELLP does not define the seizure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Abruption presents with vaginal bleeding and abdominal pain, not seizures.

questions.stem: A researcher is estimating how many pregnant patients in the United States will develop preeclampsia each year. Approximately what proportion of pregnancies in the United States are affected?

explanation.summary: Preeclampsia affects 2%-6% of US pregnancies; eclampsia is far rarer at about 0.1%.
explanation.whyCorrect: Preeclampsia occurs in 2%-6% of pregnancies in the United States. Eclampsia is much less common (8-10 per 10,000 births, about 0.1%), and HELLP occurs in 0.1%-0.6% of all pregnancies.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 0.1% is the frequency of eclampsia, not preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is within the range for HELLP in all pregnancies, not preeclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preeclampsia is more common than 1% of pregnancies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: This overstates preeclampsia; 10%-15% is the share of preeclampsia patients who develop HELLP.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation has an eclamptic seizure that stops after magnesium sulfate is given. Her family asks why delivery is being arranged. Without delivery, which of the following maternal complications is she at risk of?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cholelithiasis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gestational diabetes mellitus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hyperthyroidism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intracerebral hemorrhage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Iron-deficiency anemia

explanation.summary: Untreated eclampsia can cause intracerebral hemorrhage, temporary blindness, or cardiopulmonary arrest in the mother.
explanation.whyCorrect: The most crucial step in eclampsia is delivery, which removes the underlying cause. Otherwise eclampsia can cause intracerebral hemorrhage, temporary blindness, or cardiopulmonary arrest in the mother and intrauterine asphyxiation in the fetus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gallstones are not a complication of eclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gestational diabetes is not a complication of eclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hyperthyroidism is not a complication of eclampsia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Iron deficiency is not a complication of eclampsia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has hemolysis with schistocytes, a platelet count of 70,000/mm3, an AST of 420 U/L, and an ALT of 360 U/L. Which of the following best explains her transaminase elevation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bile duct obstruction by migrating gallstones

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct viral infection of hepatocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fatty infiltration from chronic alcohol use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hepatocyte necrosis from endothelial damage

explanation.summary: In HELLP, liver enzymes rise because hepatocytes undergo necrosis as part of endothelial damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: In HELLP syndrome, elevated liver enzymes reflect hepatocyte necrosis occurring as part of the endothelial damage that drives the disorder, which is thought to be triggered by an abnormal placenta as in preeclampsia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Autoimmune cholangiopathy is not the mechanism in HELLP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Obstruction is not the mechanism of liver injury in HELLP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viral hepatitis does not explain schistocytes and thrombocytopenia in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alcohol is not implicated in HELLP.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation has anemia with schistocytes, elevated transaminases, and a platelet count of 58,000/mm3. Her bone marrow is not examined. Which of the following best explains her thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Autoantibodies against platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased marrow production of megakaryocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Destruction within inflamed, obstructed vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dilution by expanded plasma volume

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration from portal hypertension

explanation.summary: In HELLP, platelets are destroyed by inflammation and obstruction within damaged blood vessels.
explanation.whyCorrect: The low platelets of HELLP syndrome result from platelets being destroyed by the inflammation and obstruction within damaged vessels, part of the same endothelial dysfunction that fragments red cells into schistocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated destruction is not the mechanism described for HELLP.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HELLP thrombocytopenia is from peripheral destruction, not marrow failure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dilution does not explain platelets this low with hemolysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sequestration is not the mechanism in HELLP.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 35 weeks' gestation with suspected HELLP syndrome has a peripheral smear showing numerous triangular, helmet-shaped, and comma-shaped red cell fragments with pointed edges. These cells indicate which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iron-deficiency microcytic anemia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sickle cell hemolytic anemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia

explanation.summary: Schistocytes on the smear indicate microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, the H in HELLP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hemolysis in HELLP is a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. Red cells fragmented by hemolysis are schistocytes and can be triangular, helmet shaped, or comma shaped with pointed edges.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Iron deficiency does not produce schistocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sickle cells are not the fragmented cells of HELLP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B12 deficiency produces macrocytes, not fragments.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Warm autoimmune hemolysis produces spherocytes, not fragmented cells.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman at 33 weeks' gestation comes to the emergency department with right upper quadrant pain and nausea. Her blood pressure is 128/82 mm Hg and was normal at every prenatal visit. Hemoglobin is 8.9 g/dL, platelet count is 64,000/mm3, AST is 380 U/L, and ALT is 330 U/L. A peripheral smear shows schistocytes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eclampsia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gestational hypertension

choices.label: C
choices.text: HELLP syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Preeclampsia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral hepatitis

explanation.summary: Unlike the other hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, HELLP syndrome can occur with normal blood pressure.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypertension is present in most cases of HELLP syndrome, but it is not required; HELLP has been documented in patients with normal blood pressure. Hemolysis with schistocytes, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets make the diagnosis. Every other disorder in this group requires elevated blood pressure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eclampsia requires seizures and hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gestational hypertension requires elevated blood pressure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Preeclampsia requires blood pressure above 140/90 mm Hg.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hepatitis does not explain schistocytes and thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman at 36 weeks' gestation with HELLP syndrome develops sudden worsening right upper quadrant pain, right shoulder pain, and hypotension. Imaging shows a large blood collection beneath the capsule of the organ in the right upper quadrant. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute cholecystitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatic hematoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pancreatic pseudocyst

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perforated duodenal ulcer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic rupture

explanation.summary: Hematoma of the liver is a serious complication of HELLP syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Serious complications of HELLP syndrome include DIC, placental abruption, acute kidney failure, pulmonary edema, and hematoma of the liver. A subcapsular blood collection in the right upper quadrant with hypotension fits a liver hematoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cholecystitis does not produce a subcapsular blood collection and is not a listed HELLP complication.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A pseudocyst is not a blood collection beneath a right upper quadrant organ capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perforation causes free air, not a subcapsular blood collection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spleen lies in the left upper quadrant.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman with HELLP syndrome is actively bleeding during delivery. Her platelet count is 28,000/mm3. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for her thrombocytopenia?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythropoietin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intramuscular vitamin K

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intravenous iron

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral folic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Platelet transfusion

explanation.summary: Platelet transfusion is given to HELLP patients with active bleeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delivery is the definitive treatment for HELLP syndrome, and platelet transfusion is given to patients with active bleeding to address the thrombocytopenia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythropoietin stimulates red cells and acts too slowly for bleeding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vitamin K does not raise the platelet count.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Iron does not correct thrombocytopenia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Folate does not address acute thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman who has had untreated high blood pressure since 26 weeks' gestation has an ultrasound at 34 weeks showing an estimated fetal weight below the 10th percentile. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chromosomal aneuploidy in the fetus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Congenital infection acquired in the first trimester

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fetal hyperinsulinemia from maternal hyperglycemia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maternal antibodies against fetal red cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced placental delivery of oxygen and nutrients

explanation.summary: Hypertension in pregnancy can restrict fetal growth because the fetus depends on adequate blood flow for oxygen and nutrients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gestational hypertension may affect fetal development because the fetus requires adequate blood flow to receive oxygen and nutrients. Fetal growth restriction is one listed complication of untreated hypertension in pregnancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Nothing suggests aneuploidy; her hypertension explains the finding.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nothing suggests infection; her hypertension explains the finding.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fetal hyperinsulinemia causes overgrowth, not restriction, and is unrelated to hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Alloimmunization causes fetal anemia, not growth restriction from hypertension.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with chronic hypertension who stopped her medication 2 years ago is now at 10 weeks' gestation. Her blood pressure is 150/96 mm Hg and, 4 hours later, 148/94 mm Hg. Urine protein is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Give magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis now

choices.label: B
choices.text: Start hydrochlorothiazide and monitor through pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Start labetalol and monitor closely through pregnancy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Start lisinopril and monitor closely through pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start losartan and monitor closely through pregnancy

explanation.summary: Chronic hypertension in pregnancy may be treated above 140/90 mm Hg with a pregnancy-compatible drug and close monitoring.
explanation.whyCorrect: For chronic hypertension, pregnancy-compatible antihypertensive therapy is initiated or titrated, with close monitoring of mother and fetus; medication may be indicated above 140/90 mm Hg to avoid complications. Labetalol is a preferred agent, whereas ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and thiazides are avoided.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Magnesium is for preeclampsia with severe features or eclampsia, not chronic hypertension.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Thiazide diuretics are dangerous in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ACE inhibitors are dangerous in pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ARBs are dangerous in pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation by dates has vaginal bleeding. Transvaginal ultrasound shows a uterus filled with innumerable small cystic spaces and no fetal parts. Cytogenetic analysis of the evacuated tissue shows a 46,XX karyotype in which every chromosome is paternal in origin. Which of the following best explains how this lesion arose?

choices.label: A
